3 no-DB context tests (awaited / raced / detached child shard inheritance); 7 `parse_shard_placement` tests + `handle.rs` error-conversion test; 9 DB/HTTP tests in the new `autumn-harvest-plugin/tests/shard_placement_integration.rs` (three genuinely separate shard databases: explicit-pin observability, residency-key pin, the conformance metric, unpinned-is-unchanged, and the four rejection paths — each asserting the row exists on the intended shard **only** and that a rejection starts nothing); and the real-worker e2e `worker_child_of_a_shard_pinned_parent_inherits_the_parents_shard` proving AC4 end to end through worker persistence. Registered in `.github/ci/integration-suites.txt` for the Docker-backed Linux run; all DB tests were additionally **executed green against a real local Postgres 16** (Docker unavailable in this sandbox), with the two AC4 fixes confirmed RED against the pre-fix code. **Post-review hardening (four review agents: replay/determinism, sharding-invariants, security/API-contract, and tests/AC-evidence — all findings addressed):** (1) **P1 — placement discarded on a deferred start.** A `shard_id`/`residency_key` on a **debounced** (#499) or **batched** (#518) workflow was silently ignored: those admit a start without creating an execution, so the placement had nothing to apply to and the eventual scanner-fired run hashed by the debounce/batch key. Combining them is now a `400` with a failed audit row, mirroring the three sibling deferred-start mutual-exclusion guards. A **throttled** (#607) start is deliberately excluded — it defers the same concrete placement to its scanner, so a pin there is honoured. (2) **P1 — silent residency breach on a routable-but-unpooled shard.** The start path resolved its connection through `HarvestDbPool::pool_for`, which **falls back to the default shard's pool**. The router's shard set and the pool map are configured independently, so a shard the router accepts with no pool of its own (a real state mid a shard-add rollout) would have written residency-bound data to the **default** database while the response, the encoded `ExecutionId`, and the row's `shard_id` column all claimed the pinned shard. New `HarvestDbPool::exact_pool_for` (no fallback) + `db_conn_for_pinned_shard` make the **pinned** branch fail closed with a `503`; the unpinned branch is untouched. Proven RED: reverting the branch yields `201` with `shard_id: 3` and an `ExecutionId` encoding `0003` while the row lands on EU's database. (3) **P2 — a committed keyed replay must survive its shard being drained.** Placement resolution is split into `resolve_placement` (readable **and** writable — the placing path) and `resolve_placement_for_lookup` (readable only), so the #808 committed-replay probe can still resolve its shard and return the original `200` after the pinned shard is drained; the writable check is re-applied, by delegating back to the router, only on the genuinely-fresh path. (4) **P2 — rejection messages enumerated the deployment.** `Display` stays rich for operator logs, but the HTTP body now uses a new `ShardPlacementError::client_message()` that names only what the caller asked for and never the shard set, drain state, or declared key list — a start endpoint is often reachable by a lower-trust caller than the operator surfaces. The full error is logged via `tracing::warn!`. (5) **P2 — unbounded `residency_key`.** Capped at `MAX_RESIDENCY_KEY_LEN` (128) at the request boundary so a caller-supplied string is not reflected back unbounded. (6) `ShardPlacement` and `ShardPlacementError` (enum **and** per-variant) are `#[non_exhaustive]`, `with_residency_map` trims keys on insert and warns when a declared target is readable-but-drained, and `ShardRouter::is_writable` was added. **Test-evidence hardening (from the tests/AC-evidence review):** the success metric's *"and remain on across children/CAN"* clause and CAN inheritance had **no** falsifying test — the CAN mint site was audited by reading only. Added the real-worker e2e `worker_pinned_child_and_continue_as_new_successor_stay_on_the_pinned_shard` (one run spawns a child **and** continues-as-new; asserts the encoded `ExecutionId` **and** the row's `shard_id` for both descendants, on a **non-default** shard 5 so a `default_shard` regression is caught too — confirmed RED at `ShardId(65535)` vs `ShardId(5)`); `workflow_retry_stays_on_the_predecessor_shard` for the #523 retry path (non-default shard 6, confirmed RED); `child_timeout_race_inherits_the_parents_shard` for the #779 child-or-deadline race; four `WorkflowHandleClient::resolve_shard_placement` unit tests (it previously had **zero** callers and zero tests); `routable_but_unpooled_shard_fails_closed_503_and_writes_nothing`; and `negative_and_sentinel_shard_ids_are_rejected_400_over_http` (previously parse-layer only). The reset fixture's source shard moved from `0` — which was that suite's *default* shard, so it could not catch a "always use `default_shard`" regression — to a non-default shard. Two non-falsifiable assertions were removed/repaired: `post_start` now parses the body **strictly**, so a `text/plain` `400` fails (AC6 says *400 JSON*, and every rejection test's `body.get("execution_id").is_none()` was trivially true against `Value::Null`), and a `row_count(.., ExecutionId::new())` assertion that counted rows for a random never-inserted UUID (unconditionally `0`) was replaced. The placement suite is now **13** DB/HTTP tests. `docs/sharding.md`'s rejection table was corrected to the messages callers actually receive, and gained the fail-closed `503`, the deferred-start and rollout-ordering caveats, the residency-key cardinality note, and an explicit statement that `signal-with-start`/`update-with-start` and the in-process SDK start APIs carry **no** placement field (a documented residency gap, not a silent one); `docs/security-posture.md` gained a "Data residency and shard placement" section stating that `shard_id` is **not** a capability — placement selects a database, it does not authorise access to one. **Post-review hardening round 2 (Codex bot review of PR #1138 — two P1, two P2, all fixed):** (1) **P1 — a pinned committed-replay probe could resolve out of the DEFAULT shard's database.** The #808 committed-replay probe resolved its connection with `pool_for`, whose default-shard fallback is exactly what fix (2) above closed on the *fresh-start* path — but the probe was missed. For a **pinned** request at a routable-but-unpooled shard the probe would therefore query the default database, and a same-key claim living there (from an earlier unpinned start) would be returned as a successful replay **echoed as belonging to the requested residency shard** — a silent cross-shard breach on the read path. The probe now uses `exact_pool_for` when a placement was requested (returning `None` = probe MISS, so the caller falls through to the fresh pinned path and fails closed with `503`); the unpinned branch keeps `pool_for` byte-for-byte. Proven RED: reverting it returns `200` with `"shard_id": 3` and an `execution_id` encoding shard `0000`. (2) **P1 — a shard above `0xFFFE` silently truncated through the `ExecutionId` encoding.** `ShardId::new` is unbounded (`i32`) but `ExecutionId::new_for_shard` masks with `& 0xFFFF`, so a router (mis)configured with e.g. shard `0x1_0000` would accept a pin to it and mint ids that read back as shard `0` — placing residency-bound data in the wrong jurisdiction while every observation surface agreed with the caller. New `shard::MAX_ENCODABLE_SHARD` (`0xFFFE`) + `shard::is_encodable_shard`, checked at the **top** of `validate_pinned_shard` (so it rejects even when the router is configured to accept the value) and mirrored at the HTTP boundary in `parse_shard_placement`. The reserved `0xFFFF` sentinel is rejected for a *different* reason — it round-trips byte-for-byte but means "no shard encoded, fall back to the default shard" — and the two cases are pinned separately. (3) **P2 — conflicting residency keys that collide after trimming.** `with_residency_map` trims keys on insert, so two raw keys differing only in whitespace normalise to one entry; from an unordered source which mapping survived could vary across restarts, breaking the AC3 stable-mapping guarantee (and potentially moving work between jurisdictions). The builder now takes `impl IntoIterator` and **panics** on a post-trim duplicate that disagrees on the shard, consistent with `ShardRouter::new`'s documented boot-time panic contract; a duplicate that *agrees* is accepted. (4) **P2 — a throttled deferred start did not echo its pin.** A throttled (#607) start honours a placement — the resolved shard is threaded into `reserve_or_defer` — but its `202` body omitted `shard_id`, so a caller had no way at all to audit where a deferred pinned start would run (there is no `execution_id` to decode yet). The `202` now carries `shard_id` when placement was requested and omits it entirely otherwise, keeping an unpinned deferral byte-identical to a pre-#697 build. All four are covered by falsifiable tests confirmed RED against the pre-fix code: `pinned_committed_replay_probe_never_falls_back_to_the_default_shard` and `throttled_deferred_start_echoes_the_pinned_shard` (+ the `unpinned_throttled_deferred_start_omits_shard_id` control) in the placement suite — now **16** DB/HTTP tests — and `shard_outside_the_encodable_range_is_rejected_even_when_configured`, `encodable_shard_predicate_matches_the_uuid_round_trip`, `conflicting_residency_keys_that_collide_after_trimming_panic`, plus a duplicate-agreeing control in `shard.rs`. **Post-review hardening round 3 (Codex bot review of `697d0fa`, one P2):** the operator-facing effective-config snapshot (issue #695) reported only `readable_shards`/`writable_shards`/`default_shard`, so two replicas deployed with **conflicting residency maps** serialized identically while placing the same `residency_key` in **different jurisdictions** depending on which replica served the request — the highest-blast-radius misconfiguration this feature can have, and invisible. `ShardTopologyView` gains a `residency_map: BTreeMap<String, i32>` projection (`BTreeMap`-ordered, so a byte diff across replicas is meaningful; the keys are operator-declared jurisdiction labels, never caller input or credentials, and the endpoint is admin-gated — a deliberate asymmetry with the *rejection* path, which still never enumerates the declared key set to a lower-trust start caller). **Root cause was a missing coverage guard, not a missed line:** #695's exhaustive-destructure guard covers `WorkerConfig` but `ShardTopologyView::from_router` had none for `ShardRouter`, so the `residency_map` field this PR introduced slipped through silently. Closed with a **two-hop** guard — new `ShardRouter::parts() -> ShardRouterParts<'_>` (re-exported from `lib.rs`) destructures `Self` exhaustively, and `from_router` destructures `ShardRouterParts` exhaustively, both with **no `..`** — so a new placement-affecting router field is a compile error at *both* hops until surfaced. Both hops were verified by temporarily adding a probe field and confirming `E0027 pattern does not mention field` fires at each. `docs/sharding.md` gains a "Verifying fleet consistency *before* accepting pinned starts" section with the `jq -S`/`diff` recipe; `docs/api-contract.json`'s `/admin/config` description updated. Test: `shard_topology_surfaces_the_residency_map_so_replica_drift_is_visible` builds two routers with identical topology but **mirrored** maps and asserts the topology fields compare equal while `residency_map` differs — the projection is what makes the drift detectable — plus byte-stability across calls.
- **Per-key activity rate limits** (implemented) — see issue #699. Extends the static per-activity rate limiter (#332) so an activity's rate-limit bucket key is resolved **per-execution from the workflow input** (dot-path), giving each tenant its own RPS bucket instead of sharing one cluster-wide bucket. Mirrors the per-key concurrency design (#247) and the workflow-start throttle's composite-key reuse of `harvest_rate_limit_buckets` (#607). **Declaration**: new nested `#[activity(rate_limit(key = "input.tenant_id", rps = 50, burst = 10))]` attribute (modelled on `#[workflow(concurrency(key = …, limit = …))]`; `key` and `rps` required, `burst` optional) or `ActivityInfo::rate_limit_key_expr` directly. The pre-existing **flat** `rate_limit_rps`/`rate_limit_burst`/`rate_limit_key` attributes are unchanged (AC3). The nested form is **rejected at compile time on `local = true` activities** (mirroring `circuit_breaker`) — local activities bypass the dispatch path where rate limiting is enforced. **New `ActivityInfo` field** `rate_limit_key_expr: Option<&'static str>` (the dot-path; presence selects dynamic mode). All workspace `ActivityInfo` construction sites initialise it to `None`. **Composite-key scheme**: `queue::dynamic_rate_bucket_key(expr, resolved: Option<&str>) -> "dyn-rate:{expr_component}:{resolved_component}"` — namespaced by both the key *expression* and the resolved *value* so activities declaring the same expression share one bucket per resolved value (matching the static limiter's "same key → shared bucket → must agree on rps" rule), while distinct tenants get independent buckets. The distinct `dyn-rate:` prefix can never collide with a static key (bare activity name / user string) or a throttle key (`start-throttle:`). An execution whose key expression cannot be resolved (missing / null / non-object input) is passed as `None` and falls back to a shared `dyn-rate:{expr}:U` bucket (the distinct `U` marker) so it is still bounded, not unbounded — kept **distinct** from `Some("")`, a legitimately-resolved empty-string tenant (which buckets under `dyn-rate:{expr}:L0:`), so a malformed/missing input never cross-throttles a real empty-string tenant (Codex round-5 P2; see the post-review bullet below). The `expr` is **normalized** by stripping a leading `input.` (so `key = "input.tenant_id"` and `key = "tenant_id"` — which `resolve_concurrency_key` treats as the same field — share one bucket and are validated together), and **both** the normalized `expr` and the resolved value are **length-bounded** (`MAX_KEY_COMPONENT_LEN = 256`, via the shared `bound_key_component` helper): a component longer than the bound is replaced with a stable, **collision-resistant SHA-256** digest so a pathological resolved value (a giant tenant id) *or* a pathological expression (a very long dot-path / hand-built `ActivityInfo.rate_limit_key_expr`) can never blow the `harvest_rate_limit_buckets` btree PRIMARY KEY size limit and wedge the enqueue transaction in a retry loop. With both components bounded the whole composite key is **provably ≤ ~530 bytes** regardless of the macro or a hand-built `ActivityInfo`. The key is **injective by construction** (post-review, Codex P2): `bound_key_component` emits each component as either a **length-tagged literal** `L{byte_len}:{value}` (self-delimiting: after the `L`, the decimal length up to the next `:` says exactly how many bytes follow) or a **fixed-width collision-resistant hash** `H{64hex}` (full 256-bit SHA-256, hex-encoded). The `L`/`H` first-byte tags are **structurally disjoint**, so (a) a literal value that happens to equal a hash's string encoding never collides with that hash — the earlier `h:{digest}` hash form was itself a valid short literal, so a long value hashing to digest `D` and a short literal value equal to the string `h:{D}` produced the same component (cross-tenant sharing without a hash collision), now closed because a literal `H0123…` encodes to `L{len}:H0123…` while the hash stays `H0123…`; and (b) a `:` inside `expr` (a dot-path can address a JSON key containing `:`) or inside `resolved` can never split ambiguously — the `(expr, resolved)` pair maps to exactly one key and vice-versa, whether either component passed through unchanged or was hashed. Without this self-delimiting encoding, `key = "a"` + resolved `"b:c"` and `key = "a:b"` + resolved `"c"` would both flatten to `dyn-rate:a:b:c` — two genuinely-distinct exprs colliding onto one bucket, and because builder validation keys on the (normalized) expr, their independently-validated (possibly different) rps configs would collide first-writer-wins. **Resolution at the worker enqueue site** (`worker::persist_scheduled_activities`): when `activity.rate_limit_key_expr` is `Some`, the key is resolved against the **workflow input** (`WorkflowExecution.input`, the plain start input, threaded into the function) via `concurrency::resolve_concurrency_key` and set as `params.rate_limit_key`. The static path is unchanged when `rate_limit_key_expr` is `None`. **Lazy bucket registration** (`queue::ensure_rate_limit_bucket`, shared with the static startup registration): the composite bucket is `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING`-registered in the **same enqueue transaction** so the fail-closed `EXISTS` gate in `queue::claim_task` (and the circuit-breaker dispatch-time `try_consume_rate_limit_token`) always has a bucket row to read (else the task would stall forever). `refill_rate = rate_limit_rps`, `burst = rate_limit_burst.unwrap_or(rps)`. Static-limiter startup registration skips dynamic-key activities. **Claim / gate / debit unchanged**: `claim_task` keys entirely off the row's `rate_limit_key` value and is static-vs-dynamic agnostic. The circuit-breaker split (#369) is preserved — a breaker activity skips the claim-time gate and consumes at dispatch via `try_consume_rate_limit_token`, which now holds the composite key and works unchanged (its bucket exists because it was ensured at enqueue). **Cardinality landmine fixed** (team convention / ADR-0001 §7): `record_rate_limit_throttled` uses its argument as a metric **label**, and a composite dynamic key embeds unbounded tenant input. The metric is now labelled by the **bounded activity name** (`METRIC_LABEL_ACTIVITY`), never the raw bucket key — at the dispatch-defer site (`worker::process_activity_task`, passing `activity_name`) and the sampler site (`queue::check_throttled_keys` now returns distinct bounded `activity_name`s, not raw keys). The `harvest.rate_limit.throttled` metric's label changed from `key` to `activity` (BREAKING for operators — see post-review hardening below). The per-key token/refill **gauges** are separately fixed to exclude the unbounded key families (post-review #1). **Builder validation** (`validate_rate_limit_keys`): a dynamic-key activity without `rate_limit_rps` → `RateLimitKeyWithoutCap`; two activities declaring the same `rate_limit_key_expr` with different rps/burst → `RateLimitKeyMismatch`. Dynamic keys are validated in an **independent map keyed on the expression**, so a static key and a dynamic key_expr sharing the same string are never conflated. **SQLite guard** (`autumn-harvest-sqlite`): a dynamic-key activity is rejected at registration with the same unsupported-feature error as the static form. **Management API (AC7)**: `GET /admin/rate-limits` already enumerates all bucket rows, so composite `dyn-rate:…` keys appear automatically — no new surface; covered by a plugin HTTP test. A single-key fetch (`GET /admin/rate-limits/{key}`) works for a composite key too, but the key contains `:` and (for a nested path) `.`, so it **must be URL-encoded** in the path. **Post-review hardening** (issue #699 review): **BLOCKER — per-key gauge cardinality (#1)**: the per-key token/refill **gauge** sampler (`worker::spawn_rate_limit_sampler`) emitted the bucket `key` as a metric label with no filter, so an unbounded `dyn-rate:{expr}:{tenant}` key (buckets are never GC'd) would create one time-series per tenant forever. The sampler now runs through `queue::sample_rate_limit_buckets`, whose SQL excludes the unbounded key families (`RATE_LIMIT_GAUGE_SAMPLER_FILTER` = `WHERE key NOT LIKE 'dyn-rate:%' AND key NOT LIKE 'start-throttle:%'` — the pre-existing throttle family, #607, is the same class of unbounded caller-resolved key and was silently exposed too, so it is excluded here as well). Bounded static keys keep their per-key gauges; per-tenant bucket state is observable via `GET /admin/rate-limits`, not metrics. **BREAKING metric-label change (#2)**: `harvest.rate_limit.throttled` is now labelled `activity` (bounded) instead of `key` — any dashboard/alert keyed on the old `key` label must move to `activity`. The starter-pack dashboard panel, the anti-drift ground truth (`dashboard_pack_docs.rs`), and ADR-0001 §7 are updated. **Worker-level resolution test (#3)**: a worker-driven DB test proves the composite key is resolved from the **workflow input**, not the activity's own input — two executions of one workflow/activity that differ only in workflow input (`{"tenant_id":"acme"}` vs `{}`) resolve to `dyn-rate:L9:tenant_id:L4:acme` and the unresolved fallback `dyn-rate:L9:tenant_id:U` respectively, while the activity input is identical for both. **Coupled key-set with bucket-ensure (#4)**: `params.rate_limit_key` is stamped only inside the `if let Some(refill_rate)` block, so a dynamic key is never set without its bucket being ensured in the same transaction (a stamped key with no bucket row would stall the fail-closed claim/dispatch gate forever). **`input.` prefix normalization (#6)** and **resolved-key length bound (#5)** — see the composite-key scheme above; both spellings share one bucket and are validated together, and an oversized resolved value is hashed. **Flat + nested rejected at macro parse time (#7)**: combining the flat `rate_limit_rps`/`rate_limit_burst`/`rate_limit_key` attributes with the nested `rate_limit(...)` form is a compile error (they configure the same bucket incompatibly); trybuild fixture `rate_limit_flat_and_nested.rs`. **Concurrency-contention safe-side test + documented known limitation (#9)**: `claim_task`'s `rate_limit_debit` CTE debits a token even when the `claimed` UPDATE matches 0 rows because a per-key concurrency (`concurrency_key`) advisory-lock race was lost. This is a **pre-existing** (byte-identical to trunk `claim_task`), **safe-side** (it over-throttles — the invariant "a real call always holds a token" is never violated; the leak only ever reduces dispatch below budget, never allows a claim without a token), **bounded** (≤1 token per lost claim), and **self-healing** (refills within one interval) leak, shared with the static-rate + concurrency path. The `claim_task` SQL is deliberately **not** modified (all reviewers praised its byte-for-byte invariant, and the fix would touch the hot path for a harmless-direction edge); documented in a code comment near the CTE and covered by a two-connection advisory-lock-contention DB test asserting RUNNING count never exceeds the cap nor the rate budget. **Burst-fairness success-metric test (#10)**: a 10:1 burst DB test drains tenant A's bucket to 0 while B's is full and asserts B is claimed at exactly its burst while A is never claimed (zero cross-key bleed), making the headline "one noisy tenant cannot starve another" falsifiable. **Dynamic-form builder error wording (#11)**: a dynamic-key activity missing `rps` now returns `RateLimitKeyExprWithoutCap` (names `rate_limit(key = "…", rps = N)`), not the static `rate_limit_key … remove the rate_limit_key` wording. **Key delimiter injectivity (#13, and the follow-up Codex P2)**: the composite key is now **injective by construction** via self-delimiting, structurally-disjoint per-component encodings (`L{len}:{value}` literal / `H{64hex}` SHA-256 hash, `dyn-rate:{expr_component}:{resolved_component}`) rather than relying on `expr`/`resolved` being `:`-free or on the earlier ambiguous `h:{digest}` hash form — see the composite-key scheme above for the full rationale, the `key = "a"` + `"b:c"` vs `key = "a:b"` + `"c"` collision, and the literal-equal-to-a-hash collision it closes. The **payload-offload landmine (#14)** is noted below. **Both key components length-bounded (Codex P2)**: the earlier fix bounded only the *resolved* value, leaving the *expression* unbounded — a very long dot-path or a hand-built `ActivityInfo.rate_limit_key_expr` could push the composite btree PRIMARY KEY past Postgres's ~2704-byte limit, so `ensure_rate_limit_bucket`'s `INSERT` would fail and roll back the enqueue transaction (the workflow can't schedule its activity). The bound-or-hash logic is now factored into a shared `bound_key_component` helper applied to **both** the normalized `expr` and the `resolved` value, and the injective length prefix is taken over the *bounded* expr component — so the whole PK is provably ≤ ~530 bytes regardless of the macro or a hand-built `ActivityInfo`. Distinct oversized exprs still hash to distinct keys (no cross-tenant bleed). **`dyn-rate:` prefix reserved from static author keys (Codex P2)**: a static `rate_limit_key` is an unrestricted author string; a value like `rate_limit_key = "dyn-rate:L9:tenant_id:L4:acme"` would collide with the generated dynamic bucket for `rate_limit(key = "tenant_id")` tenant `acme`, and since static and dynamic keys are validated independently and both register `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, they'd race first-writer-wins on the shared bucket's rate/burst. A static `rate_limit_key` beginning with the reserved `dyn-rate:` prefix is now **rejected at the macro parse site** (compile error; trybuild fixture `rate_limit_key_reserved_prefix.rs`), **in `HarvestBuilder::try_build`** (`RateLimitKeyReservedPrefix`), **and — for a worker built via a direct `HandlerRegistry` that bypasses both — in the worker path itself** (Codex P2, second review round): `persist_scheduled_activities` returns `HarvestError::Config` (failing the schedule/suspension transaction, so no `ActivityScheduled` event and no task row — the activity is never enqueued under the colliding key) and `register_rate_limit_buckets` logs a `tracing::error!` and skips the colliding bucket at startup, consistent with the round-3 dynamic-no-rps guard which likewise lives in both places. This keeps the static and dynamic bucket namespaces provably disjoint on every start path. Covered by a worker-driven DB test asserting the workflow never completes and neither the activity task row nor the colliding bucket row is ever registered. (The `start-throttle:` prefix from #607 is a separate pre-existing namespace; this PR reserves only `dyn-rate:` — the one it generates — and leaves `start-throttle:` as a follow-up.) **Invalid dynamic key without `rps` fails loudly at schedule time (Codex P2)**: `HarvestBuilder::try_build` rejects a dynamic `rate_limit(key = "…")` with no `rps` (`RateLimitKeyExprWithoutCap`), but an application that builds the public `HandlerRegistry` **directly** bypasses that validation, so an `ActivityInfo { rate_limit_key_expr: Some(..), rate_limit_rps: None, .. }` could reach `persist_scheduled_activities`. Because the composite-key stamping and bucket-ensure both sit inside the `if let Some(refill_rate) = activity.rate_limit_rps` block (item #4 above), such an activity previously left **both** `params.rate_limit_key` and `dynamic_rate_buckets` unset and was silently enqueued with **no** rate limit — the exact failure a rate-limiting feature exists to prevent. `persist_scheduled_activities` now guards this: an activity with `rate_limit_key_expr.is_some() && rate_limit_rps.is_none()` returns `HarvestError::Config` **before** the stamping block, failing the schedule/suspension transaction (which rolls back — no `ActivityScheduled` event, no task row, so the activity is never enqueued unrated) rather than proceeding unrated. The failure surfaces loudly (logged `tracing::error! "task execution failed"`; the suspension-persist error propagates via `persist_workflow_outcome`'s non-terminal `Err` branch, so the task is re-dispatched and re-errors on the same invalid config — a loud retry-loop, strictly better than a silent no-limit, and only reachable on an unvalidated direct-registry build). A defensive `tracing::error!` in `register_rate_limit_buckets` also surfaces the invalid declaration at worker startup, before the first enqueue. Covered by a worker-driven DB test asserting the workflow never completes and the activity task row is never enqueued. **Comprehensive rate-limit validation at worker startup (Codex round-5 P2)**: the public `HandlerRegistry` path bypasses ALL `HarvestBuilder::try_build` rate-limit validation, so an invalid config slipped through and was only caught piecemeal (or not at all) by the schedule-time guards. Rather than keep bolting on per-case schedule-time guards, the whole class is now validated **once at the fallible `Worker::new` startup boundary**: the builder's validation is factored into a shared `builder::validate_activity_rate_limits` (accepting an iterator of `&ActivityInfo` so both the builder's `Vec` and the registry's `HashMap::values()` validate without an owned copy — `ActivityInfo` is not `Clone`), and `Worker::new` calls it (mapped to `HarvestError::Config`) before its poll loop and first enqueue. This also closes two gaps the schedule-time guards never covered: (a) a dynamic `rate_limit(key = …)` on a **local** activity — which the `#[activity]` macro rejects at parse time but a hand-built `ActivityInfo` bypasses, silently running unrated inline via `run_local_activity_inline` — now rejected with the new `HarvestBuilderError::RateLimitKeyExprOnLocalActivity` (Codex worker.rs:4693); and (b) two activities sharing a normalized key-expression with **conflicting rps/burst**, whose shared `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` bucket would otherwise be insertion-order dependent (Codex worker.rs:4826). The schedule-time guards in `persist_scheduled_activities`/`register_rate_limit_buckets` remain as **defense-in-depth** behind this primary startup gate. Scope: the local reject covers the **dynamic** form only; the pre-existing static-rate-on-local #332 asymmetry stays a documented follow-up. Covered by direct-registry startup tests (`worker_startup_rejects_dynamic_rate_limit_on_local_activity`, `worker_startup_rejects_conflicting_rps_for_same_key_expr`, `worker_startup_accepts_valid_direct_registry`, plus the reframed dynamic-no-rps / reserved-prefix startup tests). **Unresolved key distinct from an empty-string tenant (Codex round-5 P2, worker.rs:4720)**: `resolve_concurrency_key` returns `Some("")` for a real empty-string tenant (`{"tenant_id": ""}`) and `None` for missing/null/non-object input, but the enqueue site's `.unwrap_or_default()` collapsed **both** onto the same `L0:` fallback bucket — cross-throttling malformed/missing executions against a legitimate empty tenant. `dynamic_rate_bucket_key` now takes `resolved: Option<&str>` and encodes `None` as the structurally-disjoint single-byte `U` marker (`dyn-rate:{expr}:U`) while `Some("")` still encodes as `L0:` (`dyn-rate:{expr}:L0:`), so the two are provably distinct buckets (the `U`/`L`/`H` first-byte tags keep the whole composite key injective). The worker call site passes `resolve_concurrency_key(...).as_deref()` through instead of `.unwrap_or_default()`. Covered by `dynamic_rate_bucket_key_none_unresolved_is_distinct_from_empty_string_tenant` and the updated absent-field worker-resolution assertion. **Collision-resistant SHA-256 digest for oversized key components (Codex P2, queue.rs:150)**: `bound_key_component`'s oversized (`H…`) form originally used a 64-bit `seahash::hash`, which is NOT collision-resistant against tenant-influenced input — two distinct >256-byte resolved values (or expressions) sharing a 64-bit digest would silently share one `dyn-rate` bucket (the `L`/`H` tags fix *format* collisions, not *digest* collisions). The `H` form is now the **full 256-bit SHA-256** of the component's UTF-8 bytes, hex-encoded (`H{64hex}`, 65 bytes; the `sha2` crate is already an unconditional `autumn-harvest` dependency, used by `payload_store.rs`/`completion_callback.rs`), so a digest collision is computationally infeasible and distinct oversized components get distinct buckets in practice. The `H` first-byte tag (disjoint from `L`/`U`) is preserved, so injectivity and the literal-vs-hash disjointness are unchanged; the composite key stays well under the ~2704-byte btree PK limit (both-oversized ≈ 140 bytes). `seahash` usage elsewhere (shard routing, jitter, build-id hashing, history-export digests) is untouched — only this tenant-facing bucket-key component needed collision resistance. The oversized-component tests recompute the expected digest via SHA-256; the disjointness test asserts the fixed 65-byte `H{64hex}` width. **Reject non-finite / non-positive rate & burst in the shared validator (Codex P2, builder.rs:2330)**: the shared `validate_activity_rate_limits` (now run by both `try_build` and `Worker::new`) only checked that a dynamic key *had* an rps — not that `rate_limit_rps` (and `rate_limit_burst`, when set) is finite and strictly positive, which the `#[activity]` macro enforces universally (`n <= 0.0` → compile error). A direct-registry `rate_limit_rps: Some(0.0)` therefore started the worker, created a `burst = tokens = 0` bucket, and left every scheduled dynamic activity permanently unclaimable (the token gate can never reach 1). The validator now rejects any activity (static OR dynamic — the macro's positivity check is universal) whose `rate_limit_rps`/`rate_limit_burst` is `!is_finite() || <= 0.0` with the new `HarvestBuilderError::RateLimitRateNotPositive { activity, field }` (stricter than the macro: also catches `NaN`/`±inf`, which `n <= 0.0` alone lets through). Because it runs at both boundaries, the `HarvestBuilder` and the direct-`HandlerRegistry`/`Worker::new` paths are both covered. Covered by `worker_new_rejects_non_positive_dynamic_rate_limit_rps`, `worker_new_rejects_non_positive_or_non_finite_rate_limit_burst`, and `worker_new_accepts_valid_positive_dynamic_rate_limit`. **Forward-looking payload-offload note (#14)**: if the start-path `WorkflowStarted` input is ever routed through the large-payload claim-check offloader (#524), `WorkflowExecution.input` would be a small reference envelope rather than the real input object, so a dynamic key would resolve to `None` and land in the shared `dyn-rate:{expr}:U` fallback bucket for every such execution. That is deterministic (no replay bug) but degrades per-key isolation to a single shared bucket; the resolution site should inflate the offloaded input first, or resolve the key before offloading, when that path lands. **Pre-existing asymmetry (follow-up, not fixed here)**: the **static** rate-limit attributes are NOT rejected on `local = true` activities (only the new dynamic `rate_limit(...)` form is). A static rate-limited local activity silently bypasses rate limiting (local activities run inline, off the dispatch path). Flagged as a follow-up. **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no replay/determinism impact, no shard-routing change.** Buckets and enqueue are **shard-local** (consistent with per-key concurrency #247 and the activity limiter): a documented, out-of-scope limitation is that cross-shard global rate coordination is not attempted, so a key's effective rate across a multi-shard cluster is `per-shard-rate × shards` (see `docs/sharding.md`). **Tests**: pure unit tests for `dynamic_rate_bucket_key` (`queue.rs`); macro-expansion tests for the flat (AC3) and nested forms + two trybuild compile-fail fixtures (`rate_limit(...)` on `local = true`, `rate_limit(key = …)` missing `rps`); builder-validation tests (dynamic-without-rps, same-expr mismatch, matching/distinct exprs, static/dynamic independence); DB integration tests in `autumn-harvest/tests/integration/rate_limit_key_tests.rs` (cross-tenant isolation / success metric, shared bucket, defer-not-fail AC6, lazy registration, static-unchanged AC3, compose-with-#247-concurrency AC8); plugin HTTP integration test (`GET /admin/rate-limits` lists the composite key).
- Partial availability for cross-shard fan-out READ endpoints (issue #756). Before, a single unreachable shard's pool turned every cross-shard **read** endpoint into a whole-request `500`: each fanned-out loop did `acquire_conn(shard_pool).await?` inside `iter_shards()`, so one down shard `?`-propagated into a top-level error even though the other shards' data was readable. Now these endpoints **collect-and-continue**: a reachable shard's rows still flow, an unreachable shard is named in a machine-readable `unavailable_shards`, and the endpoint returns `200 OK` with the union plus a `status` verdict rather than failing wholesale. **Writes keep strict failure semantics**, and the single-execution business-id resolver (#805) keeps its `503`-to-avoid-false-`404` behavior. **Reuses the existing `shard_fanout` scaffold** rather than reinventing partial-availability. New shared, pure, unit-tested helper `shard_fanout::collect_fanout_rows(observations) -> FanoutRows<R>` (`{ rows, status: FanoutStatus, unavailable_shards: Vec<UnavailableShard> }`) flattens per-shard `ShardObservation<R>`s into the union of reachable rows plus a `complete`/`partial`/`unavailable` verdict, alongside the existing `expected_shards`/`pools_by_shard`/`summarize_shard_errors`/`FanoutStatus`/`UnavailableShard` used by `workflow_count`/`usage`/`workflow_reachability`. A new async `api.rs::observe_shards(api_state, query_shard)` helper drives the collect-and-continue fan-out across `expected_shards` (so a router-known but pool-less shard mid a shard-add rollout is reported `unavailable`, never silently omitted), and `api.rs::fanout_list_json(items_key, rows, status, unavailable)` serializes the conditional envelope. The duplicate `api::UnavailableShard` struct (structurally identical to `shard_fanout::UnavailableShard`, used by the external-handoff coverage) was removed so the partial-availability shape is single-sourced. **Response-shape design — conditional envelope for bare-array endpoints, additive fields for object endpoints (deviation from the initial "envelope-always" sketch, driven by AC3 + a large consumer audit).** The five legacy **bare-array** list endpoints — `GET /workflows` (standard default + the `?no_progress_minutes` stalled loader), `GET /workers`, `GET /admin/schedules`, `GET /dead-letters`, and `GET /dags` — keep their **byte-for-byte bare-array shape on the happy path** (every shard reachable, `status == complete`) and only switch to the `{ <items>, status, unavailable_shards }` envelope **when degraded** (`status != complete`). This is the literal reading of AC2 ("*every degraded* response carries the indicator") + AC3 ("no breaking change for existing clients on the happy path"): wrapping the default bare array unconditionally would (a) be a genuine breaking change for external clients that parse the default `GET /workflows` array — which AC3 forbids — and (b) break ~57 internal test assertions across 6+ files (`workflow_filter_integration.rs`, `stalled_workflow_tests.rs`, `api_scheduler_integration.rs`, `batch_operations_integration.rs`, `build_routing_ui_integration.rs`, `legal_hold_integration.rs`) that parse those responses via `.as_array()`. The conditional switch keys on `status != FanoutStatus::Complete` (not `unavailable_shards.is_empty()`) so a degenerate `Unavailable`-with-empty-`unavailable_shards` verdict still surfaces as an envelope, never a silently-empty bare `[]`. The three **object** shapes get the two fields **additively (always present, `complete`/empty on the happy path)**: `GET /workflows?paginated` (`WorkflowListPage` gains `status` + `unavailable_shards`), `GET /workers/health` (`FleetHealth` fields stay top-level, `status` + `unavailable_shards` inserted alongside via a manual `serde_json::Value::Object` map insertion — no field collision, core `FleetHealth` untouched), and `GET /dead-letters/aggregate` (the pre-#385 hard-`?` fan-out is now collect-and-continue; `DlqAggregateResponse`'s fields stay top-level with the two additive fields inserted the same way — core `merge_dlq_aggregates` unchanged). The `GET /dead-letters` runbook-enrichment secondary read was also made best-effort (skip a shard that goes unreachable mid-request rather than `500`). **Total storage-layer unavailability is an honest `503`, not a `200 []`.** `observe_shards` guards on `storage_pool()` up front: when no pool is installed at all (misconfiguration or the boot window) it returns `503 Service Unavailable` — we cannot even enumerate shards, so a bare `200 []` would mask a whole-storage outage. Per-**shard** unreachability still degrades to `200 partial`. A router-known but pool-less shard mid a shard-add rollout is resolved exactly (`pools.get(&shard_id)`, mirroring the #805 business-id resolver), **never** through `ShardedDbPool::pool_for`'s default-shard fallback (which would silently query the DEFAULT shard's DB in its place, duplicate default-shard rows, and let `status` falsely read `complete`); it is folded into `unavailable_shards` instead. **Consumer audit finding:** the Vantage UI (`ui.rs`) queries the shard DBs *directly* (it does not consume these HTTP JSON endpoints), so wrapping the JSON never affects UI rendering — the only internal Rust caller of `load_workflows_from_shards` (the UI workflow list) reads `.executions` and shows reachable-shard rows on a partial read, and now also renders a "⚠ Partial results" banner naming the unreachable shard(s) so a partial list is not mistaken for the authoritative fleet state. The `harvest` CLI is a generic passthrough that renders whatever JSON returns; on a degraded cross-shard read (`workflow list`/`worker list`/`schedule list`/`dlq list`/`dag list`) it emits a `WARNING: cross-shard read is partial; N shard(s) unavailable: <id>: <reason>, …` notice on **STDERR** (new `fanout_partial_notice` helper, `eprintln!`'d by the caller) — keeping **STDOUT** a clean, parseable body (`-o json | jq`) on both the happy and degraded paths, so programmatic consumers of the partial-availability data are not corrupted by a prepended warning line. **Scope:** Tier 1 (the seven AC1-named loaders + `GET /dags`) is fully converted: `load_workflows_from_shards` (→ `WorkflowFanoutPage` + pure `build_workflow_fanout_page`), `load_stalled_workflows_from_shards` (→ `FanoutRows` + pure `build_stalled_fanout`), `load_schedules_from_shards` (→ `FanoutRows` + pure `build_schedule_fanout`; now the single source of truth shared by both `list_schedules` and `list_dags`, so `GET /dags` degrades and neither duplicates the query + effective-name sort), `load_dead_letters_from_shards` (+ pure `build_dead_letter_fanout`), `aggregate_dead_letters`, `list_workers_handler`, and `workers_health`. Tier 2 (`GET /audit`, `GET /workflows/summaries`, `GET /admin/schedules/decisions`) is **deferred** to keep the PR reviewable and the contract churn bounded — each is a clean candidate for the same pattern but adds contract/CLI/test surface; noted as follow-up. The internal `query_running_count` scheduler read is deliberately left fail-loud (it's a correctness counter, not an operator read). **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no shard-routing change** — this is entirely a plugin-layer read-path shape change. The eight cross-shard write loops (`batch_reset_workflows`, `create_completion_trigger`, `set_schedule_paused`, `delete_schedule`, `bulk_replay_from_shards`, `redrive_from_shards`, `bulk_discard_from_shards`, `replay_dead_letter_from_shards`) and the #805 `resolve_workflow_by_business_id` resolver were **not** touched. **Contract (AC6):** the two always-object endpoints (`/workers/health`, `/dead-letters/aggregate`) list `status` + `unavailable_shards` in both `management_api_response_fields()` and `docs/api-contract.json` `success_response.fields`; the five conditional bare-array endpoints (`/workflows`, `/workers`, `/admin/schedules`, `/dead-letters`, `/dags`) stay `free_form`/`None` (accurately: the happy-path response *is* a bare array) with the degraded envelope documented in each route's `success_response.description`. A new `compatibility.conditional_shape_note` carve-out documents that the conditional `array | object` 200 shape is not a break to any currently-successful response (the object form replaces a former `500`, and the all-reachable array is byte-identical). `contract_version` stays `2` (additive). The `contract_regression` cross-check (code registry ↔ JSON) stays green. **Tests:** pure unit tests for `collect_fanout_rows` (all-reachable → `complete` + row union; one-error → `partial` + named shard + other shards' rows present; all-error → `unavailable`; empty → `unavailable`) in `shard_fanout.rs`; a pure `resolve_expected_shard_pools` unit test in `api.rs` proving a router-known but pool-less shard resolves to `None` (folded into `unavailable_shards`), NOT to a default-fallback pool — a genuine regression guard against reintroducing `pool_for`; pure unit tests for the four merge/paginate fns *during degradation* (`build_workflow_fanout_page`/`build_stalled_fanout`/`build_dead_letter_fanout`/`build_schedule_fanout` each fed `[ok(shard 0, > limit rows), err(shard 1)]` and asserting correct ordering, truncation to `limit`, `next_cursor.is_some()` where applicable, `status == Partial`, and shard 1 named); CLI unit tests for `fanout_partial_notice` + `render_response` (bare array → no notice; empty `unavailable_shards` → no notice; degraded envelope → notice naming shard+reason; degraded body is clean/parseable on STDOUT with the notice separated to STDERR; happy-path bare array → no notice and no stderr notice). DB/HTTP integration suite `autumn-harvest-plugin/tests/fanout_degradation_integration.rs` (dual-mode: `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` or testcontainers): `GET /workflows` partial names the down shard + returns the reachable-shard run (AC7); happy path returns an unchanged bare array (AC3); `/workers`, `/admin/schedules`, `/dead-letters`, `/dead-letters/aggregate`, `/workers/health` all degrade to `partial` naming the down shard (AC1/AC2), with the aggregate asserting `total >= 1` to prove the reachable partial actually merged; a cross-shard **write** still fails `>=500` on a down shard (AC4); the #805 by-id read still `503`s (AC5). Registered in `.github/ci/integration-suites.txt` (one sorted line) for the Docker-backed Linux CI run. **Runbook (AC8):** a "Partial cross-shard list reads" stanza in `docs/runbooks/harvest-alerts.md` documenting the healthy-degradation contract and pointing at `GET /admin/shards/health`.
- **Docs** — Honest competitor comparison page (issue #963). **Docs-only** (implemented): New `docs/comparison.md` positions autumn-harvest against the five durable-execution engines an architect is most likely to shortlist alongside it — **Temporal, DBOS, Inngest, Hatchet, and Restate** — so an evaluator can reach a defensible include/exclude decision in one sitting without cross-referencing five vendors' marketing pages. Written in an engineering-comparison, credibility-first tone: it names harvest's own gaps plainly rather than only its strengths. **Structure:** an at-a-glance matrix (engines as columns) plus **11 per-dimension detail tables** covering every AC1 dimension × 6 engines — required infrastructure, self-host complexity, language/SDK support, programming model, determinism guarantees & tooling, versioning/safe-deploy, scheduling depth, observability surface, HA/multi-region, managed-cloud availability, and license. Three differentiator narratives (Postgres-only operations; determinism safety in depth; embedded-in-your-web-app deployment). A **"Where harvest is behind"** section naming 8 concrete gaps (Rust-only SDK, single-region/no multi-region DR, no managed cloud, Postgres-only/no pluggable persistence, incomplete Vantage UI parity, younger ecosystem, no cross-shard workflows, no first-party benchmarks). A **"Choose something else if…"** paragraph per competitor. **Evidence discipline (the falsifiable part):** every harvest _shipped_ capability cell carries a resolving phase entry and/or `#issue` link (e.g. build-ID routing #171 + percent ramp #604, `WorkflowReplayer` Phase 3.5, ND-block #603, schedules #240/#241/#337/#484/#478/#543/#350/#534/#771/#488/#499/#607, MCP tools #597, deterministic primitives #384, timeline #739, DAG run graph #690, health summary #679). **Planned** items are labelled as such against open issues (non-Rust SDK #959/#955, cross-region DR #954, data-residency shard pinning #697, benchmarks #941). Competitor cells are sourced from each vendor's public docs (linked inline), stamped **"accurate as of 2026-07-14"**, phrased neutrally, and flag anything **(unverified)** rather than papering over it; a maintenance note commits to revisiting the page each minor release. **Cross-linking:** linked from `README.md` (the "Why" intro) and `docs/getting-started/README.md` (the "Where to go next" index). Forward-references the planned Temporal migration guide (#947) with a note that the reverse link lands when that page ships — the bidirectional cross-link is currently forward-only because the migration guide does not exist yet. All internal relative links verified to resolve against real files. **No code, no event-schema surface, no `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no route/contract change, no replay/determinism impact** — a single new docs page plus two one-paragraph link insertions.
- **Tooling** — Publish the admission gate to the process-global cache in the keyed-replay gate test (fix trunk-red, issue #618 / #808). **Test-only fix — no production code changed.** After PR #1051 (issue #618/#607) merged, trunk-dev went RED on exactly one test: `autumn-harvest-plugin/tests/start_idempotency_integration.rs::keyed_replay_bypasses_a_raised_admission_gate` returned `201` where it asserted `503` at step 1 (a genuinely-fresh keyed start under a raised admission gate must be gated). Root cause: issue #618 (landed via #1014/#1051) made admission-gate enforcement **authoritative inside the CORE start primitive** — `execution::evaluate_start_gate` reads the **process-global** cache (`admission_gate::global_admission_gate_cache()`), not any api_state-local `Arc<AdmissionGateCache>`. The failing test predates that relocation (it was introduced in #992 for issue #808) and only ever armed the gate in the **api_state-local** cache via `api_state.initialize_gate_cache(...)`, never publishing it to the global static. So the inline test app's global cache was empty → the plain/keyed fresh-start path (which routes through the core `GateMode::Check`) saw no gate → `201`. The core `admission_gate_authoritative_tests` (26/26 green) and the plugin `admission_gate_authoritative_localpg` suite already do the right thing: publish the live handle with `set_global_admission_gate_cache(Some(api_state.gate_cache()))` on raise and tear it down with `set_global_admission_gate_cache(None)`. Fix: the test's `raise_gate`/`lift_gate` helpers now also publish the (interior-mutable) `api_state.gate_cache()` handle to the process-global static, and the test tears the global down to `None` at the end so sibling serial tests in the same binary (this suite runs `--test-threads=1`) are unaffected. This flips the assertion `201 → 503` and confirms the gap was purely test-harness: **production is unaffected** — the plugin publishes local→global at boot (`set_global_admission_gate_cache`), so the fresh keyed-start gate check works end-to-end in a real deployment; only the inline test app skipped the publish. **Sweep for the same class:** the whole test tree was grepped for tests that mutate the api_state-local gate cache without publishing to the global. The three `start_throttle_integration.rs` gate tests (`retry_with_a_pending_throttle_row_bypasses_the_admission_gate`, `armed_gate_blocks_fresh_creating_start_under_reuse_policy_on_empty_bucket`, `batch_retry_with_a_pending_throttle_row_bypasses_the_admission_gate`) arm only the local cache and assert `503` — but they exercise a **different, intentional plugin-local enforcement path**: the throttle/batch branches do their own `api_state.gate_cache().check(...)` *before* `reserve_or_defer` returns a `202` DEFER (issue #607 round 7 — "halt beats pace"; a DEFER returns before the core `GateMode::Check` ever runs). Their `503` provably comes from that plugin-local check (an ungated empty-bucket throttled start would be `202`, not `503`), so they read the correct cache **by design** and were deliberately left unchanged. The two authoritative suites already publish to the global. Only `keyed_replay_bypasses_a_raised_admission_gate` exercised the core global-cache path with a local-only gate. **Post-review hardening (Codex P2, line 879):** mutating the process-global gate cache from a plain `#[tokio::test]` is unsafe on two axes, both now closed. (1) **Parallel cross-talk** — this suite spins one Postgres container per test (`setup_database`), so it is genuinely parallel-capable; run without `--test-threads=1`, a concurrent sibling starting the same workflow while this test's gate was installed would spuriously `503`. Fixed **structurally**: the gate test now uses a workflow name **no sibling starts** (`order_flow_gate`). Because `check_admission` only blocks a start whose workflow name *matches* the gate's `WorkflowName(..)` scope, a sibling starting `order_flow` can never be spuriously gated even while the global handle is installed — cross-talk is impossible by construction, not merely reset-window-dependent. (2) **Panic-leak** (bites even under `--test-threads=1`) — the old teardown cleared the global only at the END of the body, so a mid-test panic would leak the installed gate into the NEXT serial test. Fixed with an **RAII `Drop` guard** that clears `set_global_admission_gate_cache(None)` on scope exit (incl. panic), replacing the bare end-of-body statement. A `TEST_SERIAL: Mutex<()>` (mirroring the admission-gate authoritative suites) serializes this test against any future gate-manipulating sibling in the same binary; the guard is declared after the serial lock so the global is torn down while the lock is still held. Validation (Docker-backed PG16): `start_idempotency_integration` **21/21 green both serially AND in full parallel** (`--test-threads=1` and default — the parallel run is the definitive proof the global-gate cross-talk is resolved), `start_throttle_integration` 19/19, and core `admission_gate_authoritative` 26/26 all green under `--test-threads=1` (no cross-test contamination from the shared global static). No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no production code change. **Inherited-fmt heal (unrelated to the gate fix):** the CI Lint job also flagged pre-existing rustfmt drift in `autumn-harvest/tests/integration/query_terminal_tests.rs` (two width-100 reflows introduced by #1054, already on trunk-dev and untouched by this PR). Since CI's `cargo fmt --all -- --check` fails on any drifting file, that file was reformatted under the pinned CI toolchain (stable 1.97.0 / rustfmt 1.9.0) in a separate, clearly-labeled commit; the reformat diff touches only that one inherited-drift file.
- **Trunk hardening** — de-flake `nd_blocked_cycle_does_not_emit_signal_unhandled` (Refs #1074). **Test-code-only.** The issue #603/#684 engine test `nd_block_tests::nd_blocked_cycle_does_not_emit_signal_unhandled` timed out intermittently on loaded CI runners. Its `wait_for_nd_block` poll helper (~20s budget) exhausted because the test relied on worker2's own timer-scan → append `TimerFired` → re-pend the parked task → claim → divergent-replay chain to complete inside the budget: the parked workflow task's `scheduled_at` had been set to the timer's original `fires_at` (`now + 300s`) at suspension, so backdating `harvest_timers.fires_at` alone (`fire_timer_now`) does not make the task re-claimable within the poll window. Fix (mirrors the already-passing sibling `divergent_replay_blocks_instead_of_failing`): call `make_task_claimable_now(&mut conn, exec_b)` immediately after `fire_timer_now(...)`, so the parked task becomes immediately claimable and worker2 replays the recorded history and ND-blocks promptly (the test now finishes in ~2s instead of racing the timer-scan chain against the 20s budget). Belt-and-braces: widen the local `wait_for_nd_block` loop bound from 400 to 800 iterations (~20s → ~40s) — this only extends how long a *failing* wait tolerates before panicking; a satisfied wait still returns early, so no passing test's timing semantics change. No production code touched. Verified 5×-green against a local Postgres 16 via `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` (no Docker in this sandbox). Refs #1074.
- **Phase 3.52** (implemented): Durable named cross-workflow mutex — `ctx.mutex` (issue #691). `WorkflowContext::mutex(key).acquire().await` durably suspends a `#[workflow]` until it holds exclusive access to `key`, returning a `#[must_use]` RAII `MutexGuard` that releases on drop / scope exit, explicit `release()`, the holder reaching any terminal state, or lease-TTL expiry (default 60s, `WorkerConfig::with_mutex_lease_ttl`) — the durable, replay-safe answer to "two executions must not read-modify-write the same shared resource at once" (a `#[workflow]` cannot reach for a `std::sync::Mutex`: it would not survive a worker restart, and holding a std lock across a durable `.await` breaks replay). Unlike per-key concurrency (#247) — which gates **admission** at workflow *start* and caps the running *count* of whole workflows sharing a key (`limit = 1` serializes the entire workflow and risks parent/child deadlock) — this gates a critical **region** *mid-workflow*, so only the section serializes while the rest of each workflow runs concurrently. **Append-only, single-event design:** a grant records exactly one new `WorkflowEvent` tail variant `MutexGranted { key, lock_seq, acquired_at }` (the replay anchor, matched positionally by `HistoryMatcher::match_mutex_granted` so no other scan's skip-list changes); release is event-less `ReleaseMutex` bookkeeping (mirroring `SetCurrentDetails`). Acquire is a **solo durable suspension** (a mixed batch with an activity/timer/child/signal command fails loud), guaranteeing `MutexGranted` lands at a clean resume cursor; replay recovers the guard regardless of which `lock_seq` was minted. **FIFO-fair** via a BIGSERIAL head-of-line waiter queue (`harvest_mutex_waiters`, `enqueue ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` preserves position across re-parks). **Lease-based crash safety:** the held lock (`harvest_mutex_locks`) carries a `lease_expires_at` + a `lock_seq` fencing token renewed by holder decision cycles; a reclaim scanner folded into `timeout::enforce_timeouts_once` reclaims an expired lease and wakes the next FIFO waiter, with release/reclaim fenced on `(holder_exec_id, lock_seq)` so a reclaimed-then-resumed old holder's release is a 0-row no-op. Every acquire/release/reclaim/sweep transaction takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(key))` **first** (advisory-first avoids an ABBA inversion between the scanner and acquire); a PAUSED holder (#383) is skipped by the reclaim scanner. **Terminal auto-release** (`sweep_terminal_holder_and_wake`) is folded into the single terminal chokepoint `completion_trigger::evaluate_triggers_for_execution` (complete/fail/cancel/terminate/timeout/poison-pill; continue-as-new sweeps explicitly; a non-terminal ND-block #603 correctly does not sweep). All mutex-table access is `to_regclass`-guarded and no-ops when the table is absent, so the migration is not added to the hand-rolled test INIT_SQL bundles. Reset of a source still holding a mutex is rejected (`WorkflowResetError::HolderHoldsMutex` → 409). **Shard-local scope** — the lock, FIFO queue, and advisory serialization all live on the workflow's own shard (contending workflows must resolve to the same shard, matching #247; cross-shard global mutual exclusion is out of scope). **Non-reentrant:** re-acquiring a held key returns `HarvestError::MutexSelfDeadlock` synchronously (checked before any history match, so a self-deadlock surfaces the same typed error live and on replay rather than hanging). `MutexHandle`/`MutexGuard` re-exported from `lib.rs` and the prelude; author-facing primitive only (exclusive-only, no reentrancy/upgrade/downgrade, no operator force-release route). **Migration** `20260714000001_harvest_mutex_locks` (`harvest_mutex_locks`, `harvest_mutex_waiters`, `harvest_mutex_lock_seq` sequence); no other migration. **Metrics** (`workflow`-labeled only — the lock key is high-cardinality tenant/entity input and is deliberately not a metric label per ADR-0001 §7; `execution.id` stays span-only): `harvest.mutex.wait_duration` (histogram, request→grant), `harvest.mutex.held_duration` (histogram, grant→release), `harvest.mutex.contention_depth` (gauge, FIFO waiter-queue length at grant) — bridged in `metrics_rs_adapter`, catalogued in `docs/telemetry.md` and ADR-0001 §7, paneled in `docs/dashboards/starter-pack-v0.1.0.json`. Tests: no-DB `WorkflowTestEnv` (acquire/contended/self-deadlock) and `WorkflowReplayer` fixtures (grant replay, 1000 varying-`lock_seq` cycles, release-before-subsequent-event, key-divergence → `NonDeterminismKind::MutexGrantMismatch`); DB `tests/integration/mutex_tests.rs` (mutual-exclusion-under-contention with a witness activity asserting max in-flight == 1, FIFO grant order, holder-crash lease reclaim, held-across-suspension-stays-held, terminal auto-release, cancelled holder/waiter cleanup, release-on-guard-drop-grants-next, paused-holder-lease-not-reclaimed, reset-rejected-while-holding, co-batch-fail-loud, early-release). Example `autumn-harvest/examples/mutex_ledger.rs` (two workflows serialize read-modify-write to the same per-account balance).
- **Activity-driven next-retry delay to honor downstream `Retry-After`** (implemented) — see issue #744. `ActivityFailure` gains `retry_after: Option<Duration>` (`#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]`, defaults to `None` for both `retryable()`/`non_retryable()` constructors) + a fluent `with_retry_after(Duration)` builder, so an activity author can hand the engine a downstream-supplied delay hint (e.g. an HTTP `Retry-After` header) instead of guessing a schedule. A retryable attempt failing with `retry_after = Some(d)` schedules the NEXT attempt at `now + d` instead of the `RetryPolicy`-computed backoff, **for that one attempt only** — the attempt counter and `max_attempts` cap are unaffected (the policy's attempt-cap gate runs strictly BEFORE `retry_after` is even consulted, so the hint can only override the *value* of an already-permitted delay, never resurrect a denied one). `non_retryable = true` always wins over `retry_after` unconditionally (checked first, short-circuits to the terminal/DLQ path regardless of any delay hint). The hint is clamped to `[0, retry_after_ceiling]` — a new `WorkerConfig::retry_after_ceiling` field (`DEFAULT_RETRY_AFTER_CEILING = 15 minutes`, configurable via `WorkerConfig::with_retry_after_ceiling`, wired into `HandlerRegistry` and threaded to the single `next_retry_delay` call site from both of its two callers in `process_activity_task`) — an over-ceiling hint clamps DOWN, never rejected; a non-positive (`<= 0`, i.e. exactly `Duration::ZERO` since `Duration` cannot be negative) or absent hint falls straight through to the policy delay. **Documented, confirmed edge case:** `ceiling = Duration::ZERO` is NOT a "disable the feature" switch — for any positive hint `d`, `d.min(ZERO) == ZERO`, so it resolves to an IMMEDIATE retry (`Some(Duration::ZERO)`), not `None`; there is no separate off-switch today (see `resolve_retry_after_hint`'s doc comment in `policy.rs`). Composes for free with `schedule_to_close` (issue #378): `delay` flows unchanged into the pre-existing `schedule_to_close_deadline_exceeded(task, delay)` check, so a hint that would cross the cross-retry deadline fires the existing `ActivityTimedOut { ScheduleToClose }` timeout path instead of requeuing — no new logic needed. **Interaction with per-activity circuit breakers (issue #369), documented not code-changed:** the breaker's rolling failure window only counts a failure toward tripping when it lands within `window` of the prior one, so a `retry_after` hint that regularly spaces attempts wider than a paired breaker's `window` can defeat trip detection; operators pairing the two on one activity should configure `window` generously above the largest expected hint (see `docs/getting-started/07-reliability-knobs.md` and `docs/runbooks/activity-circuit-breaker.md`, both cross-linked). **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no shard-semantics impact** — the retry's scheduled time is a pure queue-layer concern (`harvest_task_queue.scheduled_at`); a replay test (`retry_after_delayed_retry_history_replays_unchanged`) confirms a history containing a `retry_after`-delayed retry replays byte-unchanged, since the intermediate non-terminal failure leaves no event at all. `classify_activity_error(error, retry_policy) -> (ActivityFailure, bool)` parses the error string ONCE and returns both the recovered typed failure (carrying `retry_after`) and the non-retryable decision, so no double-parse drift risk exists between this path and the pre-existing `failure_is_non_retryable` classification. Additive minor-bump public API. Tests, TDD red→green→refactor: 7 pure unit tests on the field in `failure.rs`; 8 pure unit tests on `resolve_retry_after_hint` in `policy.rs` (incl. a 100-randomized-hints property test asserting EXACT equality to `min(hint, ceiling)` — a stronger bar than the issue's own "within ±1s" success metric — and a dedicated `ceiling = ZERO` edge-case test); 10 pure unit tests directly on `next_retry_delay` in `worker.rs` (zero I/O, exact-value assertions covering every AC2/AC3/AC4 branch on both the `Some(RetryPolicy)` and `None`-policy-fallback paths — closing a gap where this function previously had no direct coverage and was exercised only indirectly through wall-clock-tolerant DB tests); 6 DB/worker integration tests in `tests/integration/retry_after_tests.rs` (AC2 override-without-extra-attempts, AC3 over-ceiling clamp + zero-hint fallthrough, AC4 non-retryable-wins, AC5 schedule_to_close interaction, plus the replay test) — all run green against a real local Postgres 16.
- **`workflow_id`-addressed signal/cancel — continue-as-new-safe external targeting** (implemented) — see issue #751. Completes the external-workflow family (signal #244 / cancel #492 / await #757) with a fourth addressing mode: `ctx.signal_external_workflow_by_id` and `ctx.request_cancel_external_workflow_by_id` target a **business `(workflow_name, workflow_id)` pair** instead of a fixed `ExecutionId`, so a caller never has to track which `ExecutionId` is "current" for a long-lived entity workflow that periodically `continue_as_new`s (a device session, a per-tenant job queue, a subscription). Before this, a supervisor holding an `ExecutionId` captured at first-start would silently signal a **sealed `CONTINUED_AS_NEW` predecessor** forever after the entity's first rotation — the signal is durably recorded as delivered, and the live successor never sees it. **Design — resolve at delivery time, not request time (AC2/AC3), by construction.** `execution::resolve_execution_id_by_workflow_id(conn, workflow_name, workflow_id) -> Option<ResolvedRun>` picks the **active** run (state NOT terminal, `ORDER BY started_at DESC`) if one exists, else the most-recent **terminal** run, else `None`. Because `persist_workflow_continue_as_new` seals the predecessor (`CONTINUED_AS_NEW`) and inserts the successor in **one Postgres transaction**, a concurrent resolver run under READ COMMITTED can only ever observe the whole-transaction pre-image (predecessor still active) or post-image (successor active) — never a torn state where neither or both look active. The race is therefore closed **structurally**, not by locking or retrying: `signal::resolve_and_signal_by_workflow_id`/`execution::resolve_and_cancel_by_workflow_id` re-resolve on every delivery attempt (the outbox scanner's unconditional per-tick retry, mirroring #492's grace-window design), so a delivery that lands mid-transition simply finds nothing yet and is retried, and a delivery that lands just after finds the live successor. **New/widened types (core, `types.rs`).** `ExternalTarget` — `#[serde(untagged)] enum { ExecutionId(ExecutionId), WorkflowId { workflow_name: String, workflow_id: String } }` — **widens** (never replaces) the `target` field already present on `WorkflowEvent::ExternalSignalRequested`/`ExternalCancelRequested`; because `ExecutionId` itself is not adjacently tagged, a pre-#751-recorded target (a bare execution-id JSON value) still deserializes into the `ExecutionId` variant unchanged — **no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, replay-determinism preserved (AC7)**, proven by two matcher unit tests that replay a `WorkflowId`-targeted `ExternalSignalDelivered`/`ExternalCancelDelivered` history unchanged (`HistoryMatcher` matches on event *variant name*, never on target shape). Outcome enums (both non-`PartialEq` where the inner delivery struct isn't — use `matches!()`): `signal::ByIdSignalOutcome { Delivered, NoRunFound, NotRunning, RacedToSuccessor }`, `execution::ByIdCancelOutcome { Cancelled{..}, NoRunFound, AlreadyTerminal, RacedToSuccessor }`. `execution::is_continued_as_new_race(err) -> bool` detects the one benign `HarvestError::Config` shape a resolve-then-act interleaving can produce (a target sealed to `CONTINUED_AS_NEW` between resolution and the act itself) and converts it to `RacedToSuccessor` so callers retry rather than surfacing a false failure. **Context API (`context.rs`).** `signal_external_workflow_by_id(workflow_name, workflow_id, signal_name, payload)` / `..._with_idempotency(..., idempotency_key)` and `request_cancel_external_workflow_by_id(workflow_name, workflow_id)` both **self-check first** (`workflow_name == ctx.workflow_type() && workflow_id == ctx.workflow_id()` → immediate `Err` with `reason_code = "self_signal"`/`"self_cancel"`, records no history, stable across replay — AC6) and otherwise delegate to the *exact same* `signal_external_target`/`request_cancel_external_target` implementation the `ExecutionId`-targeted methods already use (issue #751's explicit design goal: one dispatch/matcher/error-construction path for both addressing modes, not a parallel one). **Delivery semantics (AC4/AC5), reusing the #492 same-shard/outbox split verbatim:** signal to a `workflow_id` whose current run is already terminal is a **genuine immediate failure** (`HarvestError::ExternalSignalFailed { reason_code: "not_running" }` — a signal's goal is never already met by a terminal target, unlike cancel); signal/cancel to a `workflow_id` with no run *ever* found is retried until the existing `unknown_target_grace_window` (`HarvestBuilder::unknown_target_grace_window`, threaded through `WorkerRuntimeConfig` into `spawn_timeout_checker`) elapses, then fails as `"target_unknown"` — never silently dropped; cancel of an already-terminal current run is a **no-op success** (the goal — "not running" — is already met, mirroring #492's exact rule). Both the worker's inline same-shard attempt (`worker::persist_external_signal_inline`) and the periodic cross-shard outbox (`timeout::attempt_signal_delivery`/`attempt_cancel_delivery`, called from `enforce_external_signals_outbox`/`enforce_external_cancels_outbox`) implement the full `WorkflowId` dispatch arm identically. **Cross-shard resolution (AC8).** `crate::shard::external_target_owning_shard(target) -> Option<ShardId>` resolves a `WorkflowId` target's owning shard via the **same rendezvous hash** (`ShardRouter::pick_for_new_workflow`) a fresh start of that `(workflow_name, workflow_id)` would use — so resolving where a `workflow_id` target *lives* needs no directory lookup and cannot disagree with where a real start would place it; for an `ExecutionId` target it's the existing O(1) `.shard()` decode. `ShardedDbPool::exact_pool_for_target(target, fallback_shard)` dispatches accordingly. The outbox's `same_pool` check (pointer-equality of the two resolved `DbPool` references) decides inline-vs-outbox exactly as it already did for `ExecutionId` targets. **No new production code was needed beyond the addressing/resolution layer itself** — the inline/outbox dispatch, grace-window enforcement, and cross-shard pool routing were all already correctly wired for the `WorkflowId` arm from an earlier session; this slice's engine work was the resolver (`resolve_execution_id_by_workflow_id`/`select_resolved_run`), the outcome enums, the context methods, and the `ExternalTarget` type widening. **Success metric (AC3), the headline proof.** Two randomized continue-as-new-race tests, each running **150** genuinely-randomized trials (randomized delay before spawning the resolve-and-act task vs. a concurrently-spawned continue-as-new task, `tokio::spawn` + a bounded semaphore): `randomized_signal_by_id_continue_as_new_race_zero_misdeliveries` and `randomized_cancel_by_id_continue_as_new_race_zero_misdeliveries`, both against a real local Postgres 16, asserting **zero misdeliveries** across all three possible outcome shapes per trial (resolve-wins-directly against the predecessor, continue-as-new-wins-with-direct-delivery-to-the-successor, and raced-then-retried-onto-the-successor) — every trial lands in exactly one of the three, and the sealed predecessor never receives anything in any trial. **A genuine test-infrastructure gap was found and fixed during this work, not a production bug**: `GLOBAL_SHARD_ROUTER` and `GLOBAL_SHARDED_POOL` are process-global statics shared across every test file compiled into the one `integration` test binary; every `WorkflowId`-targeted test in the new suite therefore explicitly re-installs a known-clean router/pool at its own start (`install_global_router(ShardRouter::single())` / `ShardedDbPool::single(pool.clone())`, following the pre-existing defensive convention in `admission_gate_authoritative_tests.rs`) rather than trusting whatever a previously-run test file left behind. Separately, the two cross-shard end-to-end tests initially hung: `enforce_external_signals_outbox`/`enforce_external_cancels_outbox` filter *caller* executions by `execs.shard_id = ANY(shard_assignments)`, defaulting to `[0]` when `shard_assignments` is empty — a caller `ExecutionId` deliberately encoded on shard 1 (to force a genuine cross-shard pairing against the mock's rendezvous-hashed target shard) was therefore invisible to the outbox scan until the test's `WorkerRuntimeConfig.shard_assignments` was explicitly set to `[0, 1]`; this is a **test-configuration gap**, not an engine defect — a real multi-shard deployment runs one worker per assigned shard with `shard_assignments` naming exactly that shard. **Tests, TDD red→green→refactor:** 9 pure/resolver-level DB integration tests in `tests/integration/workflow_id_targeted_tests.rs` — `resolver_signal_delivers_to_running_predecessor`, `resolver_signal_delivers_to_successor_after_can`, `resolver_signal_no_run_found_ever_existed`, `resolver_signal_terminal_current_run_is_not_running` (AC4: signal to an already-terminal current run is a genuine `NotRunning` failure, never a no-op), `resolver_signal_races_to_successor_exactly_mid_delivery`, `resolver_cancel_delivers_to_running_predecessor`, `resolver_cancel_no_run_found_ever_existed`, `resolver_cancel_already_terminal_current_run_is_noop` (AC5: cancel of an already-terminal current run is the mirror-image no-op *success*, never a failure — the signal- and cancel-side "terminal current run" scenarios are deliberately named and asserted differently, since AC4 and AC5 mandate opposite outcomes for the identical resolved-state shape), `resolver_cancel_races_to_successor_exactly_mid_delivery`; the 2 randomized race tests above; 9 end-to-end tests driving a real `Worker` (`worker_signal_external_workflow_by_id_reaches_running_target`, `worker_signal_external_workflow_by_id_reaches_live_successor_after_continue_as_new`, `worker_request_cancel_external_workflow_by_id_reaches_running_target`, `worker_signal_by_id_fails_target_unknown_after_grace_window`, `worker_cancel_by_id_already_terminal_is_noop_success`, `worker_cross_shard_signal_external_workflow_by_id`, `worker_cross_shard_cancel_external_workflow_by_id`, `worker_self_signal_by_id_rejected_end_to_end`, `worker_self_cancel_by_id_rejected_end_to_end`) — **20/20 green** against a real local Postgres 16 (Docker unavailable in this sandbox; CI runs the suite Docker-backed). **Lint hardening:** a full `cargo clippy -p autumn-harvest --all-features --tests -- -D warnings` pass (pedantic/nursery lints enabled workspace-wide) surfaced 10 pre-existing findings introduced by this slice — none behavioral: a missing `# Errors` doc section on `signal_external_workflow_by_id_with_idempotency`; `ByIdCancelOutcome::Cancelled`'s `CancelledWorkflowExecution` field boxed to shrink the enum (248 bytes → the size of the next-largest variant); `match_external_signal`/`match_external_cancel` changed to take `&ExternalTarget` instead of consuming it by value (equality comparisons only, never moved); `attempt_cancel_delivery`'s 8 arguments collapsed to 6 by bundling its three deferred-trigger/metrics accumulators into one `CancelDeliveryAccumulators` out-param struct; five `match_same_arms` findings resolved by merging `Ok(NoRunFound | RacedToSuccessor) => None`-shaped arms with the trailing `Err(_) => None` catch-all (worker.rs's signal- and cancel-by-id dispatch arms, timeout.rs's signal- and cancel-outbox delivery functions); and one `needless_borrows_for_generic_args` in a unit test. Clean pass confirmed after fixes. Example: `autumn-harvest/examples/workflow_id_addressed_supervisor.rs` (a `job_pool` entity workflow that accumulates signalled jobs and periodically `continue_as_new`s, alongside a `pool_supervisor` that signals-then-cancels it addressed *only* by its stable `workflow_id`, across any number of rotations — AC9). **Out of scope (per issue, unchanged):** idempotency keys beyond what #521 already provides on the signal path, targeting a specific *historical* run by `(workflow_id, exec_id)` (the existing `ExecutionId`-targeted methods already cover this), cross-namespace addressing, broadcast/fan-out, and `workflow_id`-addressed **await** (issue #757's `await_external_workflow` remains `ExecutionId`-only — signal-and-cancel-only per #751's scope).
- **Runtime pacing overrides for declared rate limits and start throttles** (implemented) — see issue #945. Extends the existing declared per-activity rate limiter (#332/#699) and workflow-start throttle (#607) with a **TTL'd, self-expiring runtime override layer**, so an operator responding to a downstream quota change no longer needs to redeploy or restart workers to temporarily raise or lower a bucket's pace — and never needs to remember to revert it. **Storage.** One additive migration (`20260724000000_harvest_pacing_overrides`) adds three nullable columns to the existing `harvest_rate_limit_buckets` table — `override_refill_rate DOUBLE PRECISION`, `override_burst DOUBLE PRECISION`, `override_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ` — layered on top of an existing bucket row's declared baseline (`refill_rate`/`burst`) without touching either. **Mechanism — enforced entirely at read time, no sweeper, no cache, no restart.** The override is applied via `COALESCE(CASE WHEN override_expires_at > NOW() THEN override_x ELSE NULL END, x)` inlined directly into the SAME SQL every consumer already runs: `queue::claim_task_query`'s token-availability check for activity dispatch, `queue::try_consume_rate_limit_token`'s debit for circuit-breaker-gated dispatch (#369), and the new `queue::effective_rate_limit_expr`/`resolve_effective_rate_limit` read helpers backing the extended `GET` routes.
