  ## Review round 55

  **P1 accepted — round 54's own gate covered only half the ways a worker goes
  absent.** `may_claim_tasks` is seeded from `register_in_fleet`'s **startup**
  result, so it engages when registration never committed at boot. It does not
  engage on the *runtime* path: `do_heartbeat_tick`'s `Ok(0)` arm exists precisely
  because a fleet row can vanish later — an operator cleanup, a retention sweep, a
  truncated table — and re-registers to heal it. When that heal failed, the arm
  logged a warning and left the flag clear, so the worker kept claiming while
  absent from `harvest_workers`. That is the identical end state round 54 was
  written to prevent, reached by a different route.

  The harm is the one round 54 recorded, unchanged. The worker is invisible to a
  peer's fleet evidence, so an incapable claimant can derive
  `AllLiveWorkersMissed` and terminally fail work this worker can run; and its own
  claims match `orphaned_running_tasks_query()` — `RUNNING` rows whose `worker_id`
  has no fresh heartbeat — so `reclaim_orphaned_tasks` burns a `crash_strikes`
  increment on each until `poison_pill_threshold` quarantines the task and fails
  the workflow, manufacturing a #367 quarantine out of a capability problem.

  The failure arm now arms the flag, which does two things at once: it gates
  claiming until a later tick commits the pair, and it routes that tick through
  the **top-of-function** retry rather than back through `Ok(0)` — the same heal,
  but carrying the reused-`worker_id` protections round 49 and round 51 added
  (withdraw the unverified row; never refresh a row known to be wrong). The
  success arm clears the flag, because a worker that heals itself must be able to
  claim again without a restart.

  Verified RED on the exact assertion. The failure is forced the way a contended
  database would produce it — a second connection holds the row the invalidation
  half must update and `lock_timeout` fires — rather than by injecting an error
  the production path cannot generate, and the test asserts the precondition (the
  pair really did roll back) so it cannot pass on a no-op. The control leg runs
  the identical tick with nothing blocking and requires the gate to stay **open**,
  so a fix that armed unconditionally fails it.

  Refactor: the heal is now `heal_missing_worker_row`, extracted so the gate
  transition has a name and a place to carry its rationale — and because the arm's
  new failure handling pushed `do_heartbeat_tick` past the 100-line clippy bound.

  ## Review round 56

  The first `Test (ubuntu-latest)` leg to *complete* on this branch in many rounds
  (every earlier run was cancelled by a newer push) reported two failures. Both
  are test-side; neither is a defect in the release path.

  **The cross-type continue-as-new AC5 test was asserting the pre-#804 contract.**
  Round 45 reclassified the first claim by a worker lacking a `continue_as_new_as`
  target handler: rather than sealing the predecessor, that worker now RELEASES
  the task for a capable peer — the canonical rolling-deploy shape, where the old
  pod runs the source phase and only the new peer registers the target. Issue
  #803's `continuing_into_an_unregistered_type_fails_terminally_without_a_successor`
  still waited 10s for `FAILED` and matched on the old reason text, so it timed
  out deterministically. Issue #803's AC5 is unchanged and is what the test now
  pins: with no capable peer the release is *bounded*, the predecessor is failed
  terminally with a `no_capable_worker:` reason naming the missing type, and no
  successor row is ever created. The budget is set to 1 (new
  `build_runtime_worker_with_capability_miss_budget`) so the escalation lands
  inside the wait instead of paying the default 31s of backoff dwell for real.

  That test also has to make "no capable peer" true of the *registry*, not just of
  its own intent. `live_workers_on_queue_query` selects on heartbeat freshness
  alone — a `Draining` worker is a rollback away from being capable, so excluding
  it could fabricate an escalation — and every worker in that module shares the
  `default` queue. A sibling test's worker therefore reads as an untried live peer
  for the whole freshness window after it stops, which correctly *withholds* the
  escalation bound (round-38 P1). In production those pods are gone and age out;
  here the shared database keeps their last heartbeat, so the test clears the
  fleet explicitly to leave the single incapable worker it is written for.

  **The lost-claim test was starving the worker it was waiting on.** Its
  `wait_for_task_owner` polled every 25ms through helpers that establish a *fresh*
  Postgres connection per call — up to 1,200 TCP+auth handshakes in one 30s wait,
  against a database this suite shares. That storm competes for connection slots
  with the very worker the wait is waiting on, including the startup fleet
  registration that now gates claiming (round 54). The polling helpers now open
  one connection and reuse it for the whole wait, and `wait_for_task_owner` dumps
  the task rows and the worker registry on timeout rather than panicking bare —
  an empty registry is a registration that never committed, which gates claiming
  outright and is invisible from the task row alone.

  ## Review round 57

  **The claim-theft injection was starving itself, and failed silently when it
  did.** `a_claim_lost_mid_dispatch_makes_no_terminal_decision` proves the round-28
  P1: a dispatch whose task row is reassigned mid-flight must make no terminal
  decision. It does that by having the workflow body hand its own row to another
  worker in the window between `claim_task` committing and the `AfterHandler` miss
  being raised. That injection opened a *fresh* Postgres connection — a full
  TCP+auth handshake — inside that window, on a database the suite shares. Round
  56's diagnostic dump caught the consequence on the next CI run: the task ended
  `FAILED`, still owned by `pod-loses-claim`, with `capability_misses = 0` and the
  worker registered `Active` — the signature of a panicking body contained by the
  issue #782 handler-panic path, not of a suppressed escalation. The injection now
  checks a connection out of its own pre-built pool, so it reuses a warm connection
  and waits rather than failing.

  A zero-row theft was the one outcome that silently invalidated the whole test:
  the dispatch then still owned the row, the escalation was *correct* rather than
  suppressed, and the wait for the new owner timed out with nothing to say. The
  injection now asserts it reassigned exactly one row, and `wait_for_task_owner`'s
  timeout dump carries the task's `attempt`/`crash_strikes`/`capability_misses` and
  `error` alongside the execution's state and error — so whichever way the body
  fails, the failure names itself instead of arriving as a bare timeout.
- **Phase 3.x** (implemented): Guard the suspended-dispatch catch-all against a stolen mid-flight claim — see issue #1182. **Fixed.** `handle_suspended_workflow`'s catch-all branch — reached when a live workflow-task invocation suspends with an empty command set, or a command combination the worker does not know how to persist — used to call `persist_workflow_failure` directly, with **no recheck that the dispatcher still owned the task's claim**. If a dispatcher's claim was stolen mid-flight (a poison-pill reclaim of a stale/zombie worker, an operator requeue, or a concurrent claim race) while it was still working through a slow invocation, the *original* dispatcher could go on to terminally fail a task that had already changed hands — corrupting the new owner's in-flight work with a spurious `WorkflowFailed` event and a `FAILED` execution state it never earned.

  This was reported as a reproducible CI failure: `capability_miss_tests::a_claim_lost_mid_dispatch_makes_no_terminal_decision` panicked with byte-identical output on three consecutive `trunk-dev`/CI runs (a dispatcher whose claim was deliberately stolen mid-dispatch by the test harness still failed the task under its own stale ownership, instead of making no terminal decision at all).

  **The fix.** New `fail_suspended_workflow_if_still_claimed` (`worker.rs`) replaces the unconditional `persist_workflow_failure` call in the catch-all branch. It reuses the existing `commit_terminal_failure_if_still_claimed` guarantee — the same primitive issue #804's round-28 fix built for the `AfterHandler` capability-miss escalation branch — with no escalation attached: it re-derives `next_event_id` fresh under a row lock, rechecks the claim (`worker_id` + `crash_strikes`) against the *current*, not the claim-time, state, and writes the terminal `WorkflowFailed` event only if the claim is still held. If the claim has moved (`TerminalWriteOutcome::ClaimLost`), it writes nothing and logs at `info` level — the stale dispatcher makes no terminal decision, and the row's new owner is free to drive the run to completion.

  **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration.** This composes entirely from existing primitives (`commit_terminal_failure_if_still_claimed`, `PreloadedFailureHistory`, `TerminalWriteOutcome`) that issue #804 already introduced and hardened through many rounds of review; this PR is its second call site.

  **Tests, TDD red → green:**
  - The original flaky test, `a_claim_lost_mid_dispatch_makes_no_terminal_decision`, is unchanged and now passes reliably.
  - A new, fully deterministic companion test, `a_stale_dispatcher_with_zero_emitted_commands_makes_no_terminal_decision_when_the_claim_moved`, seeds a claimed task, transfers its claim via a direct SQL update (no timing race, no sleep-based injection), and calls `fail_suspended_workflow_if_still_claimed` directly under the stolen-claim condition. It asserts the strongest possible negative: no `WorkflowFailed` event in history, the execution stays `RUNNING`, and the task row is untouched under its new owner (`worker_id == "thief"`). Confirmed genuinely RED by temporarily reintroducing the unguarded call (the reintroduced bug produces exactly the corrupted state the assertion rejects), then GREEN against the real fix.
  - Full `capability_miss_tests` suite: at this point in the review, 42 of 43 pass; the one remaining failure, `peer_reregistering_mid_dispatch_is_seen_by_the_decision`, was initially (and, as the "post-review hardening round 2" section below records, **incorrectly**) suspected of being an unrelated pre-existing bug.
  - Broader regression pass across `nd_block_tests`, `pause_tests`, `poison_pill_tests`, `workflow_retry_tests`, `retry_now_tests`, `retry_after_tests`, `worker_session_tests`, `queue_pause_tests`, `queue_pause_success_metric_tests`, `scheduler_auto_pause_tests`, and `executor_span_tests` — the suites most likely to exercise ordinary suspension/dispatch/pause/termination paths near the changed call site.

  **Multi-angle review.** Three independent review passes (correctness/concurrency, test-quality/TDD-discipline, doc/style/scope) found: no correctness issues with the fix itself; no test-quality issues (determinism, on-target exercise of the fixed path, regression strength all confirmed); two style nits (doc-comment mood, `cargo fmt`), both fixed. The correctness review additionally surfaced a **broader, pre-existing** finding — the "normal"/happy-path terminal-write route (`queue::fail_task`, `queue::complete_task`, `update_workflow_execution_failed`/`_completed`, `check_paused_and_park`, and their `reject_child_continue_as_new`/`check_continue_as_new_type` callers) has **no** worker-ownership check at all, and is far more commonly reachable than the narrow branch this PR fixes. Independently re-verified by direct source reading and filed as its own issue, #1184, rather than folded into this PR — given the demonstrated historical fragility of this exact code area (30+ prior "round N" hardening fixes to the capability-miss/claim-theft machinery, several of which needed follow-up correction), it deserves its own scoped PR with a dedicated red/green test per write site.

  **Post-review hardening (Codex, P1).** `queue::claim_still_held_for_update`'s `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` guard cannot distinguish a genuine ownership transfer from a concurrent, *unrelated* transaction merely holding the row's lock for a moment (e.g. `queue::wake_workflow_task`'s `wake_requested` fallback `UPDATE`, which touches this exact row for an instant while a sibling event wakes the same execution) — both read back identically as "not ours right now". The initial cut of this fix treated every `TerminalWriteOutcome::ClaimLost` result as "do nothing", which is correct only for the first case; in the second, the task would strand `RUNNING` forever under a worker who had already made its "no terminal decision" call and moved on, with nothing left to ever re-claim it.

  The pre-existing capability-miss caller (issue #804's round-28/29 machinery) never has this gap: every path through it that withdraws — an escalation withdrawn at the commit boundary, or an ordinary release decision — always falls through to `release_capability_miss` → `queue::release_task_for_capability_miss`, a **plain** (non-`SKIP LOCKED`) `UPDATE` that blocks behind a transient lock holder instead of skipping it, then reconciles against the row's post-commit state.

  New `queue::release_suspended_workflow_claim` mirrors that established pattern exactly, minus the capability-miss-specific bookkeeping columns (this isn't a capability miss — the handler DID run, it just made no progress): a plain, ownership-guarded (`worker_id` AND `crash_strikes`) `UPDATE`, deliberately **not** `SKIP LOCKED`, that clears `wake_requested` in the same write so a wake that landed in the contention window is reconciled rather than silently dropped. It is called only *after* `commit_terminal_failure_if_still_claimed`'s own transaction (which holds the execution row first, then attempts the task row via `SKIP LOCKED`) has already committed and released every lock it held, so it is a single, standalone task-row lock acquisition — it cannot participate in the execution-row/task-row ABBA cycle `SKIP LOCKED` exists to avoid in the first place (documented on `claim_still_held_for_update` itself: its own `SKIP LOCKED` choice is deadlock-avoidance against `poison_pill::quarantine_orphan`'s task-row-then-execution-row lock order, not a throughput optimization).

  New deterministic regression test `a_dispatcher_that_still_owns_the_claim_is_released_when_skip_locked_is_a_false_positive`: holds an open transaction's lock on the task row (standing in for a concurrent wake) while a spawned dispatch races the `SKIP LOCKED` guard, confirming it reads the row as contended; releasing the lock lets the blocked release fallback proceed, and the test asserts the strongest possible outcome — the task is released back to `PENDING` with `wake_requested` cleared, not stranded `RUNNING`. Confirmed genuinely RED by temporarily reverting to the log-and-return behavior (the task is left `RUNNING` forever, exactly the stranding this fix closes), then GREEN against the real fix.

  **Post-review hardening (Codex, round 2 — three findings, all fixed).**

  **Finding 1 (P1) — the naive fix from the round above still had a latent ABBA deadlock.** Calling the blocking, non-`SKIP LOCKED` `queue::release_suspended_workflow_claim` directly from inside `fail_suspended_workflow_if_still_claimed` — which is itself invoked from *inside* `process_workflow_task`'s persistence transaction, the one that holds the **execution** row's `FOR UPDATE` lock (via `check_paused_and_park`) for its whole duration — would make this dispatch contend for the **task** row *while still holding the execution row*. `poison_pill::quarantine_orphan` (and other task-row-first actors) lock the task row first and then go on to touch the execution row. Two connections each holding one row and blocking on the other is a textbook ABBA cycle; Postgres's own deadlock detector eventually aborts one side with `deadlock detected` rather than letting either progress.

  The fix splits the guard into two calls with a hard boundary between them. `fail_suspended_workflow_if_still_claimed` now returns `Err(HarvestError::SuspendedClaimAmbiguous { task_id })` instead of attempting any release itself — a new, non-`#[non_exhaustive]` `HarvestError` variant with a `suspended_claim_ambiguous()` accessor mirroring the existing `handler_not_registered()` convention. Propagating that error with `?` out of `process_workflow_task`'s `conn.transaction::<WorkflowPersistFlow, HarvestError, _>(async |conn| { .. })` closure forces Diesel to roll back the **entire** enclosing transaction — releasing the execution row's lock and discarding every other write made earlier in the same dispatch cycle (e.g. a `clear_nd_block` bookkeeping write) — *before* any release is attempted. Only after that rollback has completed, and the `.await` on the transaction call has returned, does `process_workflow_task`'s post-transaction `match` arm invoke `queue::release_suspended_workflow_claim` standalone, holding no other lock at all. At that point it cannot be the other half of an ABBA cycle: there is no second lock left for it to be waiting on anything else while it holds.

  **Finding 2 — the whole-transaction-rollback claim needed its own proof**, since neither existing test called the guard from inside an actual `conn.transaction()` closure with anything else to roll back. New test `an_ambiguous_claim_rolls_back_every_earlier_write_in_the_same_transaction` reproduces `process_workflow_task`'s exact shape — an unrelated `UPDATE ... current_details` write followed by the ambiguous-claim guard, both inside one `conn.transaction(async |conn| { .. })` closure whose `Err` is propagated with `?`, precisely as the real code does — and asserts the unrelated write is genuinely gone afterward, not merely that the function itself returned an error. Falsified by temporarily swallowing the guard's error instead of propagating it: the test failed exactly as expected (the unrelated write survived the would-be rollback), confirming the assertion is load-bearing rather than vacuous.

  **Finding 3 — stale capability-miss evidence must not survive a release reached only after the handler already ran.** `release_suspended_workflow_claim_query`'s `UPDATE` now also resets `capability_misses = 0, capability_miss_workers = '{}'`, matching `park_workflow_task_sticky_query`'s established `reset_capability_misses = true` precedent (issue #804) rather than `release_task_for_capability_miss_query`'s (which always *increments* it, since that release specifically records the releasing worker's own incapability). This release is reached only after `handle_suspended_workflow`'s handler dispatch has already run — the handler executed, it simply made no replay-significant progress — so it is unconditionally proof of capability, and any stale evidence naming a *different*, prior worker as incapable for this frontier must not survive it: leaving it would let the next dispatcher's capability-miss decision undercount the live, unaccounted fleet by one, based on a peer this exact release just proved wrong. Covered by the existing pure SQL-shape unit test `release_suspended_workflow_claim_query_is_ownership_guarded_and_not_skip_locked`, extended to assert both new clauses.

  New deterministic ABBA-deadlock-avoidance test, `a_task_row_first_peer_touching_the_execution_row_never_deadlocks_the_release`, drives both halves of the would-be cycle concurrently and for real: connection A locks the task row and then the execution row (poison-pill's own order) while the dispatch's blocking release waits on connection A's task-row lock, holding nothing at all itself, bounded by a `tokio::time::timeout` so a regression fails loudly and immediately rather than hanging the suite. Falsified by patching the dispatch to also lock the execution row on its own connection *before* calling the release (simulating the exact broken shape Finding 1 describes): the falsified run reproduced a genuine deadlock, surfaced by Postgres itself as `Database("deadlock detected")` and by the test as a loud panic — proving the test would have caught the round-1 gap had it existed, before reverting the patch and confirming the real (fixed) code passes cleanly and repeatably.

  Full `capability_miss_tests` suite re-run after all round-2 fixes: **46 of 46 pass** (43 pre-existing + the round-1 hardening test + the two round-2 tests above). Full broader regression pass (`nd_block_tests`, `pause_tests`, `poison_pill_tests`, `workflow_retry_tests`, `retry_now_tests`, `retry_after_tests`, `worker_session_tests`, `queue_pause_tests`, `queue_pause_success_metric_tests`, `scheduler_auto_pause_tests`, `executor_span_tests`): 147 of 147 pass, no regressions.

  **Correction — `peer_reregistering_mid_dispatch_is_seen_by_the_decision` was misdiagnosed, and #1185's hypothesis was wrong.** That test was originally believed to be an unrelated, pre-existing bug and filed separately as issue #1185, with a *documented, not-yet-confirmed* lead pointing at `queue::invalidate_capability_miss_evidence_for_worker` only clearing the `capability_miss_workers` array column and never the `capability_misses` count column. Issue #1182's own tracking text names this test as part of the *same* regression, so it was investigated further as part of this PR. Extensive static analysis of the capability-miss decision machinery (`capability_miss_decision`, `fleet_capability_evidence`, `resolve_capability_miss_with_confidence`, `current_frontier_miss_state`) reached a contradiction with the observed failure, which was resolved empirically (temporary debug instrumentation dumping the failing task/execution rows): the test's `capability_misses`/`capability_miss_workers` columns were **completely unchanged** from their seeded values, proving the capability-miss decision code was never even reached, and the actual recorded error was `"workflow suspended without emitted commands; resumption is not implemented yet"` — a totally different failure mode than the one #1185 hypothesized.

  The real root cause: the test's injected workflow handler performed a raw `AsyncPgConnection::establish(url).await` (a full TCP connect plus Postgres auth handshake) directly inside the workflow body, from within `workflow_invalidates_peer_then_misses`. `executor::SUSPENSION_TIMEOUT` gives a live workflow-task invocation only 100ms to reach a genuine command-emitting suspension point; under load, establishing a fresh connection inline reliably blows that budget, tripping the very "zero emitted commands" terminal-failure path this whole PR is about — before the workflow body ever reached the capability-miss-triggering `ctx.execute_activity_raw` call the test exists to exercise. This exact anti-pattern (a raw connect inside a workflow body under the 100ms budget) is a documented, previously-fixed hazard in the same test file, via the sibling `CLAIM_THEFT_INJECTION`/`prewarm_claim_theft_injection` pattern used by an already-passing test.

  **Fix (test-only, no production code change):** `RACE_INJECTION` was converted from a `OnceLock<(String, String)>` (a raw URL) to a `OnceLock<(DbPool, String)>` (a pre-warmed connection pool), mirroring `CLAIM_THEFT_INJECTION` exactly, with a matching `prewarm_race_injection()` helper called before the worker starts. The workflow handler now checks out a pooled connection (`pool.get().await`) instead of establishing a fresh one, paying only the `UPDATE`'s round trip inside the 100ms budget rather than a full handshake. Confirmed deterministic (not flaky) both before and after: it failed identically and reproducibly on 3+ isolated runs pre-fix (including against the unmodified pre-round-1 base commit, ruling out any interaction with this PR's own changes), and passes reliably on 5+ isolated runs post-fix (consistently ~3.2s, down from the flaky ~3.7–3.8s of the failing runs). Issue #1185's stated hypothesis is now known to be incorrect and the issue is resolved by this PR rather than tracked separately.

  **Post-review hardening (Codex, round 3 — one finding, fixed).**

  **Finding (P1) — the round-2 release was still inside the issue #494 `workflow_task_timeout` budget.** Round 2 correctly moved `queue::release_suspended_workflow_claim` to run only *after* `process_workflow_task`'s persistence transaction rolled back (closing the ABBA hazard), but that whole sequence — transaction, rollback, and the standalone release — still executed **inside** `process_workflow_task`, and `process_workflow_task`'s entire future is itself wrapped in the issue #494 workflow-task-timeout budget by `run_under_workflow_body_budget` in `process_task`. `queue::release_suspended_workflow_claim` is deliberately blocking (it waits for the task row's lock rather than skipping it, per round 1's `SKIP LOCKED`-false-positive fix) — so under row contention, that wait alone could consume the remainder of the budget, get cancelled mid-flight, and report a false `TaskDispatchOutcome::BodyTimedOut` — banking an issue #494 timeout strike against a workflow whose handler had, in fact, already completed cleanly within its own budget. Only the *cleanup* afterward was waiting on unrelated row contention.

  **The fix** mirrors the established capability-miss pattern exactly (`process_task` already defers `handle_capability_miss` until after the budget unwraps, for the identical reason). `process_workflow_task`'s `Err(error) => { .. }` arm no longer intercepts `SuspendedClaimAmbiguous` at all — it now simply lets the error propagate, exactly as `HandlerNotRegistered` already does. `process_task` gained a new interception point, checked immediately after `run_under_workflow_body_budget` returns and *before* the pre-existing `handler_not_registered()` check: a new private helper, `handle_ambiguous_suspended_claim`, performs the release there — outside the budget entirely — and maps it to `TaskDispatchOutcome::Released { clears_timeout_strike: true }` (`true` because this scenario is only reached after the handler has already run to completion, the identical rule `TaskDispatchOutcome::Released`'s own doc comment already documents for the `AfterHandler` capability-miss case).

  The extraction into `handle_ambiguous_suspended_claim` was additionally required to satisfy `clippy::too_many_lines` (`process_task` was capped at 100 lines; inlining the release+logging block pushed it to 105) — a genuine, independently-useful decomposition rather than a lint-appeasing workaround, since it now gives the ambiguous-claim interception the same one-function-one-concern shape the capability-miss interception already has.

  No new regression test was added specifically for this finding: `process_workflow_task`, `process_task`, and `run_under_workflow_body_budget` are all private with zero pre-existing test call sites (unlike `fail_suspended_workflow_if_still_claimed` and `queue::release_suspended_workflow_claim`, both made `#[doc(hidden)] pub` specifically to support the round-1/round-2 tests), so exercising this exact relocation in isolation would need either new pub surface carved out solely for the test or a full in-process mock of the dispatch loop's ~16-parameter call graph (`HandlerRegistry`, `WorkflowCache`, `SessionSlotRegistry`, panic-strike maps, etc.) — disproportionate cost for a change that is a pure code-motion mirroring an already load-bearing, extensively-tested pattern. Confidence instead rests on: (1) the fix is architecturally identical to the pre-existing, heavily-covered capability-miss deferral it mirrors line-for-line; (2) the round-1/round-2 lock-contention tests (`a_dispatcher_that_still_owns_the_claim_is_released_when_skip_locked_is_a_false_positive`, `a_task_row_first_peer_touching_the_execution_row_never_deadlocks_the_release`) already demonstrate the release can take measurable, contention-bound time — exactly the scenario this fix protects against escalating into a false timeout; and (3) a full `capability_miss_tests` re-run (46/46) plus the full previously-run broader regression suites confirm zero behavioral regression from the code motion.

  Also fixed in this round, as an accuracy-only follow-up with no logic change: `docs/rnd/sqlite-feasibility.md` (issue #966's R&D report) needed its Postgres-coupling inventory updated to reflect the new `SKIP LOCKED` doc-comment references this round's code introduced — `error.rs`'s `SuspendedClaimAmbiguous` variant documents the `SKIP LOCKED` ambiguity it represents, and `worker.rs` gained additional such references. The report's own anti-drift test suite (`sqlite_feasibility_docs::`) caught this immediately in CI (`every_inventoried_module_records_the_mechanisms_grep_finds`, `mechanism_counts_quoted_in_the_report_are_current`) — `error` is reclassified from `(a)` (trivially trait-able) to `(c)` (fundamentally Postgres-shaped), joining `store` and `concurrency` as a third "comment-only consumer" of the `SKIP LOCKED` invariant (a module that references the invariant only in prose, relying on it without issuing the SQL itself — a class the report's own audited revision already celebrates catching). The skip-locked mechanism count, per-module coupling cells, and the derived `(a)`/`(b)`/`(c)` totals (7/17/19 of 43, was 8/17/18) were all updated to match; a short honesty-pass note was added acknowledging a third comment-only consumer joined the list after the report's original audit.

  Full `capability_miss_tests` suite re-run after the round-3 fix and the extraction refactor: **46 of 46 pass**. `docs/rnd/sqlite-feasibility.md`'s own `sqlite_feasibility_docs::` suite: **14 of 14 pass**. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo clippy -p autumn-harvest --all-features --tests -- -D warnings`: both clean. Full broader integration regression suite (2,142 tests): 2,134 pass; the 6 remaining failures (`child_policy_tests::terminal_detached_spawn_setup_error_fails_workflow`, `integration_e2e::worker_completes_ten_child_fan_out_within_wall_clock_bound`, `panic_containment_tests::panicking_activity_task_leaves_running_within_one_poll_interval`, `scanner_tick_db_tests::spawned_poison_pill_reclaimer_registers_ticks_and_deregisters`, `scanner_tick_db_tests::spawned_timeout_checker_ticks_all_owned_scanners_with_no_work`, `slot_tuner_tests::tuner_grows_under_load_and_drains_cleanly`) are all timing/load-sensitive tests in files that do not reference any code this PR touches (confirmed by grep), and were independently reproduced — failing identically, by name — against the unmodified committed baseline with this PR's round-3 changes stashed out entirely, confirming they are pre-existing sandbox-environment flakes unrelated to this work.

  **Post-review hardening (Codex, round 4 — one finding, fixed).**

  **Finding (P1) — the release left a stale `crash_strikes` count in place.** `release_suspended_workflow_claim_query`'s `UPDATE` already reset `capability_misses`/`capability_miss_workers` (round 2, Finding 3) on the reasoning that this release is reached only after the handler has already run to a conclusion, so it is unconditionally proof of capability and any stale evidence naming a prior worker incapable must not survive it. The same reasoning applies, unnoticed until this round, to the *poison-pill* crash-streak counter (issue #367): the `WHERE ... AND crash_strikes = $3` guard correctly pins the release to the exact claim-time snapshot (so a concurrent poison-pill reclaim that bumped the count in the interim is still detected as "the claim moved" and the release correctly no-ops), but the `SET` clause carried that same stale value forward into the released row instead of clearing it. This dispatch attempt proved the process did not crash — it ran the handler to completion and merely couldn't confirm ownership afterward — so leaving the old count in place would let an already-resolved, unrelated crash history keep counting against a task that just proved itself healthy, one strike closer to an undeserved poison-pill quarantine. `release_task_for_capability_miss_query`'s `AfterHandler` phase already resets the same column, unconditionally, for the identical "the body reached a conclusion on this worker" justification — this release was simply missing the analogous line.

  **The fix** adds `crash_strikes = 0` to the `SET` clause, alongside the pre-existing `capability_misses`/`capability_miss_workers` reset, leaving the `WHERE`-clause guard on the claim-time snapshot (`crash_strikes = $3`) completely unchanged — the guard's job is to detect whether the claim moved *before* this write runs; the reset only decides what value the row gets written to once the guard has already confirmed ownership. The function's doc comment was extended to explain the reset using the same "the handler ran to a conclusion on this worker" framing already used for the capability-miss reset immediately above it, explicitly naming `release_task_for_capability_miss_query`'s `AfterHandler` phase as the established precedent being mirrored.

  **Tests, TDD red → green:** the existing pure SQL-shape unit test `release_suspended_workflow_claim_query_is_ownership_guarded_and_not_skip_locked` was extended with a new assertion, `sql.contains("crash_strikes = 0")`. Confirmed genuinely RED against the unfixed query — the test panicked with the new assertion's message, proving the gap existed — then GREEN against the fix. No new integration-level test was needed: this is a single additive clause on an already-covered, already-executed `UPDATE` statement whose row-level effect (the released row's final `crash_strikes` value) is a direct, mechanical consequence of the SQL text itself, with no new control flow, no new caller, and no new interaction to exercise — the existing lock-contention and whole-transaction-rollback integration tests already drive this exact statement to execution against a real database on every run.

  Full `queue::tests` module re-run after the fix: **71 of 71 pass**. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo clippy -p autumn-harvest --all-features --tests -- -D warnings`: both clean. Full `capability_miss_tests` suite re-run: **46 of 46 pass**, no regressions.
- **Phase 5.1** (implemented): Backup/restore runbook and PITR restore verification tooling — see issue #943. Harvest's durability story ended at "it's in Postgres, back that up". This slice answers the question a backup does not: **after the restore, is the fleet safe to resume, and what will happen the moment workers start?**

  **New core module `autumn-harvest/src/backup_verify.rs`** — a pure vocabulary
  plus a read-only DB half (`db`-gated):

  - **Four-tier severity model.** `FindingSeverity::{Reclaimable, Advisory,
  Incoherent, Undetermined}`. Only `Incoherent` (exit **1**) and `Undetermined`
  (exit **2**) fail a drill. This tiering is load-bearing: a *correct* restore
  always contains dead-worker `RUNNING` rows and expired leases, so a tool that
  reported those as failures would cry wolf on every healthy drill and be
  ignored by the third one.
  - **`Undetermined` outranks everything, including `Incoherent`.** A probe that
  could not run found nothing *because it did not look*. The canonical case —
  caught by manually smoke-testing the real binary, not by a test — is a
  "restore" that produced an **unmigrated/empty** database: every probe errors on
  a missing table, every condition reads as absent, and a naive tool reports a
  beautiful clean bill of health on an empty database. That is the single most
  dangerous output this tool could produce, so "we could not tell" is never
  allowed to render as a pass. Regression-pinned by three pure tests
  (`an_unrunnable_probe_is_undetermined_never_a_pass`,
  `undetermined_outranks_incoherent_and_reclaimable`,
  `advisory_classes_never_escalate_the_verdict`) and the DB test
  `an_unmigrated_restore_is_undetermined_never_a_pass`.
  - **24 `FindingClass` variants** (8 reclaimable / 9 incoherent / 6 advisory / 1
  undetermined), each carrying a `const fn explanation()` that names the healing
  mechanism and its issue number, so the report teaches rather than just alarms.
  The severity table is pinned exhaustively against `FindingClass::ALL`
  (`severity_truth_table_is_pinned_for_every_class`), so demoting any single
  class — which changes the exit code, and therefore whether an operator starts
  workers on a broken fleet — fails a test.
  - **`VerifyStatus::{Clean, ResumableWithReclaim, Incoherent, Unavailable}`** with
  `const fn exit_code()` → 0 / 0 / 1 / 2.

  **Read-only by construction, three independent ways (AC4):**

  1. Every connection issues `SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION READ ONLY`
   on connect, so any write fails with SQLSTATE `25006` — a Postgres-level
   guarantee, not a code-review promise.
  2. **No mutating scanner is ever called.** The AC asks to "run the scanners once
   and report what they would reclaim", but `enforce_timeouts_once` and friends
   *mutate*. So verify reuses their **selection predicates verbatim** — the same
   `poison_pill::orphaned_running_tasks_query()`,
   `timeout::{heartbeat,start_to_close,schedule_to_start,schedule_to_close,workflow_execution}_timeout_query()`,
   `sessions::broken_session_candidates_query()`, `mutex::expired_leases_stmt()`
   `const` strings the live scanners use — and reports the rows they *would*
   claim. Sharing the `const` makes the report drift-proof by construction: a
   predicate change moves both at once.
  3. A live-DSN guard that **fails closed** — an unparseable DSN compares as
   *matching*, so a malformed connection string can never sneak past.

  Counts are exact and samples are bounded via `COUNT(*) OVER ()` computed
  **before** `LIMIT`, so a report never trades accuracy for boundedness.

  **Replay honesty.** Sampled non-terminal histories replay in **canary** mode, not
  strict: a parked in-flight run legitimately suspends at its recorded frontier, so
  strict replay would flag every healthy run in the fleet as divergent. An
  unregistered workflow type is recorded as `replay_skipped_no_handler`, never as a
  divergence, and `ReplaySummary::verified()` makes a report structurally unable to
  claim replay coverage it does not have.

  **Testing-harness additions** (`testing.rs`): `WorkflowReplayer::replay_canary_from_db`,
  `is_workflow_registered`, `registered_workflow_names`; `replay_from_db` refactored
  onto a shared private `snapshot_from_db`.

  **CLI** (`harvest backup verify --shard <[N=]DSN>… [--i-know-this-is-scratch]
  [--format text|json] [--replay-sample N] [--worker-stale-secs N]`): a local
  command (early-return in `run_cli`, `unreachable!()` in `api_request`),
  repeatable `--shard` with an optional `N=` prefix parsed so a DSN query string
  containing `=` is never mangled, `CliError::{RestoreIncoherent,
  RestoreUndetermined}` carrying the exit-code contract, and DSN redaction
  everywhere a DSN is printed. The CLI's `autumn-harvest` dependency enables `db`
  **unconditionally** (no new CLI Cargo feature), matching the house convention of
  zero `#[cfg(feature)]` in the CLI and keeping every CI lint/test leg covering the
  new code; diesel's `postgres_backend` + diesel-async/tokio-postgres are pure
  Rust, so the Windows/macOS legs stay green.

  **Multi-shard skew (AC3).** `harvest backup verify` accepts every shard in one
  invocation and cross-checks parent/child terminal ordering and external
  signal/cancel/await targets across them. A reference into a shard whose DSN was
  *not* supplied degrades to the advisory `uninspected_shard_reference` rather than
  silently passing — supplying every shard is what turns an advisory into a
  verdict. Fleet skew is reported as `restore_point_skew_secs`.

  **Runbook** `docs/runbooks/backup-restore.md`: backup approach per table class
  (`pg_dump` vs physical/PITR, and why the durable-truth class wants PITR), exact
  post-restore semantics for each in-flight artifact with the healing mechanism
  named, the **plainly stated** at-least-once consequence (any activity whose
  `ActivityCompleted` landed after the restore point *will run again*, against the
  current outside world), the 30-minute drill, how to read the four verdicts, and
  the multi-shard fencing procedure — **restore all shards, verify all shards,
  then start workers**, never one shard at a time.

  **Zero engine impact (AC5): no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no
  runtime behavior change.** This is a CLI + docs + read-mostly verification slice
  over existing primitives; the only non-CLI production edits are three additive
  `WorkflowReplayer` accessors.

  **Replay honesty.** The shipped `harvest` CLI links no application `#[workflow]`
  handlers, so its replayer is structurally empty and check (a) is **always**
  reported `NOT VERIFIED` — never silently claimed. `RestoreVerifyReport` carries
  a top-level `replay_verified: bool` so a JSON consumer can gate on it without
  re-deriving the rule, and the runbook's §4.3 leads with the limitation and gives
  the embedder recipe (call `verify_restore` from a binary that registers your
  handlers) for operators who want check (a) too.

  **Post-review hardening** (multi-angle review before submission): the severity
  table is now pinned exhaustively (a class demotion previously survived every
  test); `non_terminal_executions` became `Option<u64>` so a failed count probe
  reports `null` + `probe_failed` instead of a fabricated `0` that reads as a
  drained fleet, and a failed newest-event probe no longer silently disables the
  skew check; `probe_limit` is floored at `1` so a mis-set knob can never emit
  `LIMIT 0` and fabricate an all-clear; a new `wedged_schedule_claim` class
  (Incoherent) catches a torn claim pair (`fire_claim_token` set,
  `fire_claimed_until` NULL), which the scheduler's claim predicate can never
  match again — permanently wedged, not merely expired; the session-reclaim probe
  mirrors the scanner's Rust-side "elapsed lease but a member is still RUNNING"
  suppression instead of over-reporting; `--live-dsn` is repeatable so a sharded
  fleet is fully guarded, and a run whose guard did not actually run (no live DSN,
  or `--i-know-this-is-scratch`) now prints a `WARNING:` on stderr rather than
  being silently inert; and the runbook documents the read-only pin's
  connection-pooler caveat (session-scoped, so not durable under PgBouncer
  transaction pooling) plus the one reused predicate that is faithful by review
  rather than by construction.

  **Tests.** 22 pure unit tests in `backup_verify.rs` (including the exhaustive
  severity pin); 14 testcontainers integration tests in
  `tests/integration/backup_verify_tests.rs` seeding the issue's ≥5 incoherence
  classes plus a pristine-restore control, an AC4 never-mutates assertion that
  snapshots **state** (not just row counts) across every probed table and asserts
  the run genuinely found something, a direct SQLSTATE-25006 proof of the
  read-only pin, genuine two-database cross-shard `child_terminal_rolled_back`
  **and** `child_execution_missing` cases, the torn-claim and
  suppressed-session-lease predicate-fidelity cases, an unreachable shard, and the
  unmigrated-database false-clean regression; 22 CLI tests in
  `autumn-harvest-cli/tests/integration/backup_verify_cli.rs` plus 3 clap-parse
  unit tests. DB suites ran green against a real local Postgres 16 and are
  registered in `.github/ci/integration-suites.txt` for the Docker-backed Linux
  run.

  **Post-review hardening, round 2** (automated review of the opened PR, two
  genuine P1s plus two correctness gaps, each verified against real code before
  being fixed and each RED-probe verified by reverting the fix):

  1. **P1 — a replayed workflow error was counted clean.** `replay_sample`
   collapsed `ReplayStatus` to a divergent/clean bool, so
   `ReplayStatus::WorkflowFailed` fell into the clean bucket. But the sample is
   drawn exclusively from **non-terminal** runs, whose recorded history contains
   no terminal failure — a replay failure there means the deployed handler now
   errors where the live run had not, which is exactly what a post-restore
   verification exists to catch. The engine's own replay canary (`run_canary`
   in `testing.rs`) already counts that as `replay_failed`; verify now matches
   it. New Incoherent class `ReplayWorkflowFailed`, new `ReplaySummary.failed`
   counter (folded into `verified()`/`merge()` and the CLI's text renderer).
  2. **P1 — a resolved external request asserted nothing about its target.** The
   reference scan dropped every request that had a recorded terminal, so a
   restore that rolled the *target* shard back past a delivered signal/cancel
   read clean — the exact asymmetry the design already avoids for children via
   `ChildTerminalRolledBack`. Terminals are now split by outcome: a **failure**
   terminal (`External*Failed`) applied no effect and is still droppable, while
   a **success** terminal (`ExternalSignalDelivered` / `ExternalCancelDelivered`
   / `ExternalAwaitResolved`) asserts durable state on the target shard —
   per-effect, mirroring how the engine applies it. Cancel and await require the
   target to be terminal; a signal requires either a `harvest_signals` row (the
   `consumed` flag means rows persist after delivery) or a recorded
   `SignalReceived` event. New Incoherent class `ExternalEffectRolledBack`.
  3. **Undecodable reference events now fail closed.** A malformed, legacy or
   newer-version payload on a child/external row was silently skipped, yet that
   row may be the very reference that would have exposed a missing target. It is
   now reported as `Undetermined` (the replay sample is not a backstop: the
   shipped CLI links no handlers, and an embedded replayer samples only a
   bounded subset).
  4. **`dsn_targets_same_database` no longer misses a multi-host or `hostaddr`
   DSN.** The live-DSN guard parsed a single host/port; libpq accepts
   comma-separated `host=`/`hostaddr=`/`port=` lists, so a failover DSN could
   slip the guard. It now parses full identity lists (`DsnIdentity`) and matches
   on any overlap, with `hostaddr` taking precedence over `host` — a widening,
   so the guard can only become more conservative, never less.

  Tests: 8 new DB integration tests (22 total) covering both P1s with their
  matching clean controls — a delivered cancel whose target is terminal, a
  delivered signal with a queued row, a *failed* request asserting nothing — plus
  the undecodable-event case and a real registered-handler replay failure/success
  pair; 4 new unit tests. Both P1 fixes were confirmed falsifiable by reverting
  them and observing the corresponding test fail.

  **Post-review hardening, round 2** (automated review of the round-1 fixes; two
  genuine P1s, both in the new `ExternalEffectRolledBack` signal check, each
  confirmed against engine source before being fixed and each RED-probe verified):

  1. **P1 — a healthy restore was reported rolled back.** The signal check looked
   only at the target's own execution row, but BOTH continue-as-new
   (`worker.rs`) and workflow-level retry
   (`signal::forward_signals_to_retry_attempt`, issue #843) **reassign**
   `harvest_signals.workflow_exec_id` to the successor — the retry path moves
   the whole mailbox and re-arms `consumed`. An unconsumed signal produces no
   `SignalReceived` event, so after either transition the original target
   carries no row *and* no event, and the check reported `Incoherent` ("do not
   start workers") on a perfectly good restore. The lookup now walks the
   target's successor chain (`continued_from_exec_id` / `retry_of_exec_id`) via
   a recursive CTE. Cancel and await are unaffected — a continued-as-new target
   is `CONTINUED_AS_NEW` and a retried one is `FAILED`, both already terminal.
  2. **P1 — a repeated channel name masked a rollback.** The check matched on
   `(workflow_exec_id, signal_name)`, so a target that had received *any* signal
   of that name read clean even when the specific delivery had been rolled back
   — reopening the false-clean the class exists to prevent. A delivered signal
   is now matched **exactly by its `idempotency_key`** (issue #521), the only
   per-delivery identity the engine persists on the target side, carried into
   the reference from `ExternalSignalRequested` and normalised the same way
   `send_signal_idempotent` does (an empty key is no key). `effect_verdict`
   became tri-state: with a key the answer is definitive either way; without
   one, absence is still a definitive `ExternalEffectRolledBack` but presence
   is reported as the new **advisory** `ExternalEffectUnverifiable`. Advisory
   rather than `Undetermined` because this is a permanent precision limit of the
   data model, not a probe that failed to run — escalating it would mean the
   tool could never return clean for any fleet using unkeyed external signals,
   which would push operators to ignore it.

  Tests: 5 new DB integration tests (**27** total) — continue-as-new forwarding,
  retry forwarding, keyed-exact rollback detection, its exact-key-present clean
  control, and the unkeyed advisory (asserting it does *not* escalate the
  verdict). All four behavioural tests were confirmed RED against a reverted
  check; the fifth is a control that passes both ways by design.

  **Post-review hardening, round 3** — two more findings, both false-cleans on
  the guarantees the tool exists to provide, both fixed TDD red→green:

  1. **P1 — delivered external effects from a *terminal* caller went unchecked.**
   The cross-shard reference scan filtered owning executions to
   `RUNNING`/`PAUSED`/`SUSPENDED`. That rule belongs to the **child** checks (a
   terminal parent's awaited child may legitimately have been collected by
   retention, so scanning it would report `child_execution_missing` on a healthy
   restore) but was wrongly applied to external effects too. A caller that
   recorded `ExternalSignalDelivered` and then completed still asserted durable
   state on the *target* shard, and that assertion does not expire — if
   anything a terminal caller is the worse case, because no live caller remains
   to re-drive the delivery, so the target waits forever for a signal that
   nothing will resend. Verification exited 0 on it. The owner-state filter is
   now split by event class: external events are scanned from every retained
   caller, child events keep the narrow filter. The widening is paired with a
   `terminal_owners` guard in `build_refs` so a terminal caller's *unresolved*
   request is dropped rather than reported `external_target_missing` — nothing
   is waiting on it and its target may since have been collected, which would
   have traded one false clean for a false `Incoherent`.
  2. **P2 — an omitted `dbname` compared as the empty string.** libpq (and so the
   server, since tokio-postgres simply omits `database` from the startup packet
   when unset) defaults the database name to the **connection user**. Storing
   `""` made `postgres://harvest@prod-host` compare unequal to
   `postgres://ops@prod-host/harvest` even though both reach database
   `harvest`, so the live-DSN guard waved a production target through without
   the `--i-know-this-is-scratch` acknowledgement. The identity now resolves a
   missing `dbname` to `get_user()`. With neither present the real name is the
   connecting OS username — not knowable here and different on the operator's
   machine than in the deployed config — so the identity is refused entirely,
   which makes the guard fail closed rather than guess.

  Tests: 2 new DB integration tests (**29** total) — a delivered effect from a
  `COMPLETED` caller is adjudicated, and an unresolved request from a
  `TERMINATED` caller is *not* reported missing — plus 2 new DSN-guard unit
  tests. Each half was independently falsified: the widening was confirmed RED
  before the SQL split, and neutering the `terminal_owners` guard alone makes the
  second test fail, so both halves are load-bearing rather than decoration.

  Also fixes a CI break from round 2: three `dsn_guard_*` unit tests called a
  `#[cfg(feature = "db")]` function without carrying the gate, so
  `cargo test --no-default-features` failed to compile. The guard parses with
  `tokio_postgres::Config` — deliberately the same parser `diesel_async` uses at
  connect time — and `tokio-postgres` is enabled only by `db`, so the tests take
  the gate too.

  **AC coverage gap closed.** `RestorePointSkew` — the AC3 signal that two shards
  were restored to materially different points — had only a pure unit test
  (`compute_skew_needs_two_timestamps`); nothing exercised the detection
  end to end. Added `detects_restore_point_skew_across_shards` (two shards, one
  backdated an hour, asserting both the finding *and* the reported
  `restore_point_skew_secs`) and the control
  `shards_restored_to_the_same_point_are_not_flagged_as_skewed`, without which the
  positive test would pass even if the check fired unconditionally — which would
  make every healthy multi-shard drill report a finding. Falsified by neutering
  the threshold comparison. **31** DB integration tests.

  **Post-review hardening, round 4** (Codex, two P1s and a P2 — each verified
  against real engine source before any code changed).

  1. **P1 — a non-`COMPLETED` await terminal is a resolution, not a transport
   failure.** `execution::read_external_await_outcome` returns
   `ExternalAwaitOutcome::Terminal { reason_code, .. }` for a target that
   reached `FAILED`/`TIMED_OUT`/`CANCELLED`/`TERMINATED`, and both the worker
   (`worker.rs`) and the outbox (`timeout.rs`) record that as
   **`ExternalAwaitFailed`** — the same variant used for the genuine transport
   failure `target_unknown`. The scan bucketed the whole `*Failed` class as
   "applied no effect", so `build_refs` dropped it and a target shard restored
   to *before* the terminal the caller had observed was silently missed.
   Fixed by splitting on the reason code: the four terminal-outcome codes are
   adjudicated exactly like `ExternalAwaitResolved`; only `target_unknown` and
   `self_await` stay in the no-effect bucket. The match is deliberately an
   **allowlist of transport codes**, so an unrecognised future reason code
   falls into the adjudicated bucket — worst case a finding an operator can
   dismiss, never a silently skipped check.

  2. **P1 — `CONTINUED_AS_NEW` is not proof an await resolved.**
   `read_external_await_outcome` *follows* a `CONTINUED_AS_NEW` target through
   its successor chain and resolves only once the chain **head** is terminal.
   `effect_verdict` shared one arm for `Cancel | Await` that accepted any
   `is_terminal_state()` — which includes `CONTINUED_AS_NEW` — so a resolved
   await whose successor had been restored back to `RUNNING` read as coherent.
   `Await` now has its own `await_verdict` walking the same chain the engine
   walks (the predecessor's own `WorkflowContinuedAsNew` event, not the
   `continued_from_exec_id` back-link, which is absent on pre-#701 rows). An
   absent successor row counts as ordinary retention — the predecessor's seal
   and the successor's insert are one transaction, so an absent successor was
   terminal. `Cancel` keeps the simple terminal check, which is correct for it:
   a delivered cancel against an already-terminal target is a documented no-op
   success (issue #492), so any terminal state is consistent.

  3. **P2 — the cross-shard reference scan truncated instead of paginating.** A
   hard `LIMIT probe_limit` (default 1000) meant any fleet with more reference
   events than one probe reported `probe_failed` → `undetermined` → exit 2: a
   false "cannot verify" on a healthy restore, with no operator override (the
   CLI exposed `--replay-sample` and `--worker-stale-secs` but not
   `--probe-limit`). The scan now **pages** by keyset on the owner id, keeping
   the existing boundary-drop so no owner group is ever split, and re-fetching
   the dropped tail group from the start of the next page. Two bounded exits
   still raise a truncation note rather than reporting a clean prefix: a single
   execution carrying more reference events than one page (which cannot advance
   the cursor, and would otherwise either loop forever or skip that group
   silently), and an internal page ceiling. `--probe-limit` is now exposed and
   is a **page size**, not a ceiling. The per-page `COUNT(*) OVER ()` window
   function is gone, since completeness is now decided by a short page.

  Tests: 6 new DB integration tests (**37** total), each paired with the control
  that would pass a naive fix — `a_terminal_outcome_await_failure_is_adjudicated_not_discarded`
  vs `a_target_unknown_await_failure_asserts_no_effect_on_the_target` (without
  which "adjudicate every `ExternalAwaitFailed`" would pass);
  `a_resolved_await_whose_successor_is_still_running_is_rolled_back` vs
  `a_resolved_await_whose_successor_is_terminal_is_clean` (without which "treat
  `CONTINUED_AS_NEW` as always-lost" would pass); and
  `a_reference_scan_larger_than_the_probe_limit_is_paginated_not_truncated` vs
  `pagination_still_detects_a_rollback_beyond_the_first_page` (without which
  "page once and stop" would pass, silently narrowing the check). Plus CLI
  parse coverage asserting the new flag and that its default tracks
  `DEFAULT_PROBE_LIMIT` rather than a drifting literal.

  **Post-review hardening, round 5** (two Codex P2s, both fixed):

  1. **`--shard` accepted shard ids that cannot round-trip.** The parser rejected
   only an `i32` parse failure, so `65535` (the reserved `ShardId::UNENCODED`
   sentinel) and anything above it were accepted — but an `ExecutionId` carries
   its shard as `shard & 0xFFFF`, so `65536` truncates to `0`. Every target id
   read out of the database the operator supplied under `65536=` then decoded as
   shard 0, missed the supplied map, and was written off as "on an uninspected
   shard": an advisory, exit 0, and the shard the operator actually handed over
   never checked. `parse_shard_targets` now validates with
   `autumn_harvest::shard::is_encodable_shard` — the same rule the shard router
   uses, so the two cannot drift — and names the valid range in the error.
  2. **The embedder recipe did not compile from a default-feature dependency.**
   `ShardTarget` / `VerifyOptions` / `verify_restore` and `WorkflowReplayer` are
   gated on `db` + `testing`, and `testing` is off by default, so an application
   following runbook §4 could not import either line until it independently
   discovered the feature. The section now leads with the required
   `Cargo.toml` stanza and notes that `testing = []` pulls in no extra runtime
   dependency (so it is safe in a drill binary and can stay off in the
   production service). The `--shard` flag row also states the encodable range.

  Tests: `unencodable_shard_ids_are_rejected` (`65535` / `65536` / `70000`, each
  asserting the error names the offending id) paired with the boundary control
  `the_largest_encodable_shard_id_is_accepted` (`65534` still parses), so the
  guard rejects only what genuinely cannot round-trip. RED confirmed before the
  fix: the rejection test failed at `65535` while the control already passed.

  **Post-review hardening, round 7** (two of four Codex findings fixed here; the
  other two filed as #1205, see below):

  1. **A numeric `host` bypassed the production-DSN guard.** `parse_dsn_identity`
   put every `Host::Tcp` value in the hostname set, so candidate
   `postgres://u@10.0.0.5/harvest` and live
   `postgres://u@prod-alias/harvest?hostaddr=10.0.0.5` — the same TCP
   destination and database — overlapped in neither the hostname set nor the
   address set, and the guard permitted a verification run against production
   without the acknowledgement flag. A numeric host *is* an address: comparing
   it needs no DNS, so it now parses with `IpAddr::from_str` and joins the
   address set. That also normalises IPv6 spellings on both sides (`[0:0:…:1]`
   vs `::1`), since `get_hostaddrs()` already yields `IpAddr`. This is **not**
   the limitation the function documents — that one is a `host` *name* against a
   bare `hostaddr`, which genuinely requires resolving DNS and is still refused
   by design. The change only ever produces *more* matches, which the guard's own
   doc names as the safe direction, and the `hosts.is_empty() &&
   hostaddrs.is_empty() → None` fail-closed path is unchanged.
  2. **The embedder recipe called `exit_code` on the wrong receiver.** Round 5
   fixed the missing feature stanza but left `report.status.exit_code()`;
   `exit_code` is implemented on `RestoreVerifyReport`, not `VerifyStatus`, so
   the snippet still did not compile. Now `report.exit_code()`.

  Test: `dsn_guard_matches_a_numeric_host_against_a_hostaddr` covers both
  directions (numeric candidate vs pinned live, and the reverse), the IPv6
  normalisation, and a numeric-vs-numeric regression — paired with the control
  that a *different* address (`10.0.0.6` vs `10.0.0.5`) is still correctly treated
  as a genuine scratch target, so the widening does not simply match everything.
  RED confirmed before the fix on the first assertion; all 7 pre-existing
  `dsn_guard_*` tests still pass.

  The remaining two findings — retention being indistinguishable from a
  pre-creation rollback when a cross-shard target row is absent (P1), and
  `Finding::new` reporting `truncated: false` while clipping the sample list (P2)
  — are filed as **#1205** rather than fixed here, since this round is past the
  review-round budget agreed for this PR. Both were verified against source before
  filing. The two fixed above were treated as deliberate, narrow exceptions: a
  guard that stops a drill running against a live database is a hard constraint
  rather than a review-iteration preference, and the runbook snippet was a factual
  error in something round 5 had claimed to verify.
- **Phase 4** (implemented): Per-shard worker poll loops and scheduler ticks, finished and made falsifiable — see issue #961. Reconciliation slice in the #543/#593/#609/#753 precedent: most of the multi-shard runtime shipped piecemeal under #522 (per-shard poll loops, per-shard control loops, the stranded-work sampler), #796/#1157 (per-shard scheduler ticks, DAG->shard pinning, stale-row collection), #797 (per-shard scanner liveness) and #774 (queue coverage) — this closes the residuals and gives every AC a test that can fail.

  **Auto shard assignments (AC1, behaviour change).** An **empty** `WorkerConfig::shard_assignments` now means *auto*: cover every shard the process has a pool for. Previously it defaulted to a literal `[ShardId::new(0)]`, so a three-shard `ShardedDbPool` with no explicit `with_shard_assignments` call silently drained shard 0 and left the others permanently undispatched with no error anywhere. New pure `builder::resolve_shard_assignments(explicit, pool_shards)`; empty + **no pool preserves the empty list** rather than fabricating a `[ShardId::new(0)]` that asserts a shard number the process never established (Codex round 2 — the write-side twin of issue #1150, whose read-side consumers all normalise an empty array as "covers whatever shard the row was read from"; `ShardRouter` also accepts an arbitrary `default_shard`, so `0` is not a safe stand-in). Single-shard stays byte-for-byte unchanged (AC7): the poll loop's shard is `Option<ShardId>` and the per-shard `harvest.shard.dispatched{shard}` counter is emitted only when the worker has a shard identity, so a pool-less worker attributes no per-shard dispatch — its dispatch remains visible on `harvest.queue.dispatched{queue}` (#515). Resolution runs in `Worker::new` (and in the plugin runner right after the pool is assigned) — deliberately **not** in `From<WorkerConfig> for WorkerRuntimeConfig`, which runs before the runner assigns the pool and would therefore accomplish nothing; a regression test pins that ordering. `GET /admin/config` reports the **resolved** list (`worker.shard_assignments`), which is what the runbook's coverage check reads.

  **`with_shard_assignments(<empty>)` flips meaning.** It previously coerced to `[ShardId::new(0)]`; it now records the auto sentinel. Intended configuration is unaffected, but a **computed** list (`.with_shard_assignments(shards_from_env())` returning `vec![]` when the variable is unset) changes from "narrow to shard 0" to "fan out across every pool shard" (or, with no sharded pool, to the empty legacy shape every read-side consumer already normalises).

  **Third drifted copy of the shard-membership predicate closed.** `preflight::worker_can_cover` had its own inline `worker.shard_assignments.contains(&shard_id)` check with no empty-array normalization — issue #1150's third instance, after `shard_fanout` and `fleet_health`. It now delegates to `shard_fanout::worker_covers_shard`, so a worker on the auto default is no longer reported as covering nothing.

  **`ShardedInfo` lost `Copy`** (`effective_config.rs`) — it now carries a `shard_ids: Vec<i32>`.

  **Per-shard dispatch counter (AC5).** New `harvest.shard.dispatched{shard}` counter — the shard-dimension twin of #515's `harvest.queue.dispatched{queue}` — emitted from the two poll-loop sites that know which pool they claimed from (a task row carries no `shard_id` column; "which shard" *is* "which pool"). Standard three-touchpoint recipe plus dashboard panel, ADR-0001 §7 row, and `docs/telemetry.md`.

  **Starter alert entry (AC6).** New `harvest_shard_undrained` rule over the existing `harvest.shard.stranded_pending` gauge, with a full runbook section. Its narrow "no poller at all" variant uses `unless`, not `and ... == 0`: a shard that has never had a covering poller has no `harvest_shard_dispatched_total{shard}` series, so an `== 0` comparison drops the alert in exactly the case it exists to detect.

  **LISTEN/NOTIFY on the multi-shard path stays per-shard-URL only.** An earlier cut of this slice let the pool's *default* shard fall back to the global `notification_database_url`, to preserve the NOTIFY wake-up an auto-widened deployment previously had on shard 0. That was withdrawn on review (Codex P2): `notification_database_url` is configured independently of `sharded_pool`, so a numeric default-shard match does not establish that the URL targets that shard's database — and a pool override (`HarvestRunnerResources::with_sharded_pool`) can leave it aimed at the original `harvest_pool` entirely, opening a listener on the **wrong** database (real NOTIFYs missed, unrelated ones triggering needless claim attempts). It also contradicted the call the single-shard `global_safe` gate already documents for real multi-shard routing: *"an absent per-shard URL means poll-only for this shard rather than risking a wrong-database listener"* (#522 review). The resolver is now the pure `multi_shard_listener_url`, which takes **only** the per-shard map, so the hazard is unrepresentable rather than heuristically guarded. Consequence: a multi-shard worker with no `shard_notification_database_urls` falls back to poll-interval dispatch latency on **every** shard — a latency cost, never a correctness one (claiming always runs against the shard's own pool) — and a startup warning names the one-call fix.

  **Buffered-drain shard-encoding de-drift (AC4).** `drain_buffered_schedule_runs` gated on `schedule.dag_name.is_some()` while the main dispatch path used `scheduled_fire_encodes_shard`. Both now call one shared `scheduled_fire_exec_id`, guarded by a source-level anti-drift test. Not reachable today (the canary registers with `OverlapPolicy::Skip`, which never buffers) — it becomes live the moment an operator `PATCH`es that policy (#771).

  **Docs (AC8).** `docs/sharding.md` step 4 gained three falsifiable verification checks, and its fictional `[harvest.worker] shard_assignments` TOML block was replaced with the real Rust surface (`WorkerConfig::with_shard_assignments` / `HarvestRunnerResources::with_sharded_pool`) plus the note that multi-shard is `HarvestRunner`-only.

  **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no event-contract or replay-determinism change.** New DB suite `autumn-harvest/tests/integration/sharded_runtime_tests.rs` (real per-shard databases): auto-coverage, explicit narrowing, per-shard timeout scanner, per-shard external-signal outbox, per-shard scheduler HA over 100 contested slots per shard under two replicas, round-robin fairness against a self-replenishing backlog, stranded-shard detection (never-covered and worker-killed), DAG pinning across restart and widening, and a single-shard regression.

  **CRLF-safe source-level guard.** The AC4 anti-drift test parses `scheduler.rs` at test time to prove both fire paths mint through the shared decision; its `\n}\n` brace probe found nothing on a Windows checkout (`core.autocrlf`), so the test panicked there while passing everywhere else. It now normalizes line endings (the `sqlite_feasibility_docs.rs` convention) and — so a regression fails on *every* platform rather than only the Windows CI leg — runs the identical guard a second time over a CRLF copy of the same source.

  **`harvest.shard.dispatched` is exported by the built-in scraper too.** `HarvestPlugin::with_metrics_scrape()` installs `HarvestMetricsRecorder`, which is per-metric hand-maintained; the new counter initially fell through the trait's no-op default and so was absent from the recommended built-in Prometheus endpoint. That mattered here specifically because the `harvest_shard_undrained` alert shipped in this same PR reads `harvest_shard_stranded_pending` (already rendered by that recorder) and uses `harvest_shard_dispatched_total` to tell "no poller at all" from "poller present but backlogged" — the alert's primary signal was exported while its discriminator was not. Added as a counter family, mirroring the sibling gauge.

  **One canonical shard-membership predicate for the whole workspace.** `autumn_harvest::workers::shard_assignments_cover` now owns the "an empty assignment array covers whatever shard the row was read from" rule (issue #1150). It lives in **core**, not beside its first plugin caller, because core has consumers of its own — `apply_worker_filters` — that cannot reach into `autumn-harvest-plugin`, which is why independent copies kept drifting. `shard_fanout::worker_covers_shard` delegates to it, and two remaining literal-membership consumers were routed through it: `api.rs::evaluate_eligibility_for_shard` (which reported a healthy auto-assignment worker as `wrong_shard_assignment`) and `workers.rs::apply_worker_filters` (which omitted it from `GET /workers?shard_id=N`). A **malformed** (non-array) value still covers nothing — it is corrupt, not a legacy shape — so the eligibility check reads the raw JSON value rather than the decoded `Vec<i32>`, whose `unwrap_or_default()` would have collapsed malformed into the permissive empty shape.

  **Auto-resolution must not widen the blast radius of the existing multi-shard weaknesses (three P1s).** Auto-coverage makes the multi-shard path the *default* for any `ShardedDbPool`, which turned three latent weaknesses into default behaviour. (1) **`spawn_monitoring_tasks` fanned out quadratically.** It starts one timeout checker per assigned shard and handed every checker the *full* assignment list, but each `enforce_timeouts_once` pass iterates that list again (`fire_due_debounced_starts`, `fire_due_throttled_starts`, `fire_due_event_batches`, `fire_due_completion_deliveries`, `sweep_expired_start_idempotency`, and the three external outboxes) — so an N-shard worker performed N x N pool acquisitions and table scans every poll interval, and one unreachable shard aborted every healthy shard's remaining pass (`fire_due_event_batches` propagates its acquisition error with `?`, and completion-callback delivery plus the idempotency sweep run after it). Each monitor is now narrowed to its own shard via `monitor_shard_scope`; the union across the N monitors still covers every shard exactly once, so the pass is O(N), a shard's failure is contained to its own checker, and N checkers no longer contend on the same `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` rows. The residual — a wedged checker no longer has peers incidentally covering its shard — already applied to its own-database work and is what #797's per-shard `harvest.scanner.tick` liveness exists to detect. (2) **One unavailable pool stranded every peer shard.** Harvest configures no deadpool `Timeouts`, so every `pool.get().await` is unbounded, and the multi-shard path visits shards *sequentially* in two places: `run_multi_shard`'s startup loop (`register_in_fleet` + `register_rate_limit_buckets` per shard — a shard that never yields a connection means the poll loop is never reached **at all**) and `run_poll_loop_multi` (round-robin rotation cannot help, because the loop never reaches the rotation). Both now acquire through one `acquire_shard_conn` helper under `shard_acquire_bound`, so a bad shard costs an iteration instead of parking the loop; each site already had a graceful failure branch (the per-shard pending flag its heartbeat retries, or simply rotating on). The bound is floored at `MIN_SHARD_ACQUIRE_BOUND` (5s) rather than tracking `poll_interval` — a first cut used the poll interval directly and *starved* a shard that merely had a deep backlog, because a busy bounded pool legitimately takes far longer than one poll interval to hand over a connection. The cost is amortized, not free: an unavailable shard is re-probed once per rotation, which is degraded throughput for its peers rather than stranding; a per-shard cooldown or concurrent polling would remove even that and is a natural follow-up. (3) **The single-pool public entrypoint advertised coverage it never drained.** `run_with_listener` registers, heartbeats and polls exactly the one pool it is handed and attributes every dispatch to `shard_assignments[0]` — consistent while the default was a literal `[ShardId::new(0)]`, but auto-resolution widens an unconfigured worker to every pool shard, so a direct embedder would register a fleet row claiming N shards while draining one. That is worse than lost throughput: a worker falsely advertising coverage is exactly what suppresses this PR's own stranded-shard signals (`harvest.shard.stranded_pending`, shard health's `no_live_worker` gate), so the undrained shards would be invisible as well as idle. It now fails closed (`single_pool_entrypoint_rejects`), mirroring the fail-closed posture `run()` already takes for `missing_assigned_shard_pools`; `Worker::run` still routes a genuine multi-shard config to `run_multi_shard`, and its own internal call reaches the guard only when `use_multi_shard` is false. The guard is scoped to a configured `ShardedDbPool` — a first cut keyed on the assignment count alone and refused to start a legitimate configuration: with **no** sharded pool the shard-target resolution in `run` maps every assignment onto the caller's one pool (`pool.clone()` per assignment), so a single poll loop genuinely drains every assigned logical shard. That is the "several logical shards colocated on one physical database" shape, where the outbox's `execs.shard_id = ANY(..)` filter is the only thing that needs both ids, and refusing it stranded the very work it was meant to protect (it broke the pre-existing `worker_cross_shard_signal_external_workflow_by_id` / `..._cancel_...` tests, which are exactly that shape). The narrowing loses nothing Codex raised: auto-resolution only ever widens when a sharded pool is present, so the auto-widened case the guard exists for is still caught in full. The residual in the colocated shape is fidelity, not stranding — every dispatch is attributed to `shard_assignments[0]`, so `harvest.shard.dispatched{shard}` under-reports the other logical shards, while `harvest.shard.stranded_pending` is unaffected because the worker does advertise both shards and does poll the database holding them. That matches pre-#961 behaviour for the same config. Single-shard is unchanged throughout (AC7): `shard_acquire_bound(false, ..)` is `None`, which is the original unbounded `pool.get().await` byte-for-byte, and a one-shard config never trips the entrypoint guard.
- **Fix** — `ensure_runtime_migrations` panicking on a TLS-enabled Postgres database URL. **Bug fix** (implemented): the plugin's startup migration step (`autumn-harvest-plugin::plugin::ensure_runtime_migrations`, invoked from the `on_startup` hook's `start_harvest_runtime`) panicked unconditionally — before any network I/O — whenever the configured `DATABASE_URL` requested TLS (`sslmode=require`/`verify-ca`/`verify-full`), crashing the process on boot with `"Cannot start a runtime from within a runtime"`. A plaintext or `sslmode=disable`/`prefer` URL was unaffected.

  **Root cause.** `ensure_runtime_migrations` was a plain synchronous `fn`, called with no `spawn_blocking` wrapper from `start_harvest_runtime` — an `async fn` invoked via `.await` from the `on_startup` hook, i.e. from a thread that is already actively driving the Tokio runtime's async tasks. It delegates to `autumn_web::migrate`, which selects a migration-connection strategy per `sslmode`: a plaintext/`disable`/`prefer` URL takes the synchronous libpq `PgConnection::establish` path (safe from any thread); a TLS-requesting URL routes through `establish_migration_connection`'s rustls arm, which calls `tokio::runtime::Handle::try_current()` — succeeding by reusing the *same* ambient runtime handle — and then `handle.block_on(tls::establish(..))`. Tokio forbids nesting `block_on` on a thread already driving that runtime's own tasks and panics immediately with `"Cannot start a runtime from within a runtime. This happens because a function (like `block_on`) attempted to block the current thread while the thread is being used to drive asynchronous tasks."` — before any connection attempt completes, so the failure is deterministic and unrelated to network reachability. `establish_migration_connection`'s own doc comment states this precisely: *"Never call from an async executor thread ... Sync contexts (the CLI) and `spawn_blocking` tasks (the startup migration path) are both fine."*

  **Fix.** `ensure_runtime_migrations` is now an `async fn` that clones its (already-cheap, already-owned) inputs and runs the unchanged synchronous body — renamed `ensure_runtime_migrations_blocking` — inside `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, awaiting the join handle and mapping both a task panic/cancellation (`JoinError`) and the inner `Result` to the existing error type. `spawn_blocking` moves the closure to a dedicated blocking-thread-pool thread that is *not* marked as actively driving the runtime's scheduler, so the nested `Handle::block_on` inside `establish_migration_connection` is explicitly sound there — exactly the sanctioned pattern the doc comment above calls out, and the same pattern already used elsewhere in this codebase (`autumn-harvest::worker` wraps a similar nested-`block_on` WASM-activity invocation the same way) and in `autumn-web`'s own internal startup-migration sequence. The single call site was updated from `ensure_runtime_migrations(..)?` to `ensure_runtime_migrations(..).await?`.

  **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no route/contract change, no replay/determinism impact** — this is a pure runtime-startup bug fix confined to `autumn-harvest-plugin`.

  **Tests.** Two new unit tests in `autumn-harvest-plugin/src/plugin.rs` reproduce the hazard hermetically — no real TLS-enabled Postgres server is needed. A URL like `postgres://user:pass@127.0.0.1:1/harvest?sslmode=require` selects the TLS/rustls migration-connection path (port 1 is essentially never bound, so the connection is refused near-instantly), and the panic occurs before any connection attempt, so the fixture is deterministic:
  - `migration_body_is_safe_to_call_directly_from_an_async_context` calls the renamed synchronous body directly from an async-task context and asserts it does **not** panic. It replaces the original `#[should_panic]` reproduction fixture (`ensure_runtime_migrations_blocking_panics_if_called_directly_from_an_async_task`), which became obsolete in the autumn-web 0.7 upgrade: `with_migration_connection!` now runs both the connect and the migration body on a freshly spawned `std::thread::scope` thread, so the nested `Handle::block_on` — and with it the panic the fixture reproduced — is gone upstream. The `spawn_blocking` wrapper is retained only so the blocking join never stalls an async worker thread. The TLS fixture now uses `HarvestMode::Split`, since `Embedded` short-circuits before any connection is attempted (Autumn owns those migrations).
  - `ensure_runtime_migrations_does_not_panic_on_a_tls_requiring_database_url` calls the new async `ensure_runtime_migrations` from the same async-task context and asserts a clean `Err` result with no panic.

  Both new tests pass; the full `autumn-harvest-plugin` lib unit test suite (961 tests) is green with zero regressions. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo clippy -p autumn-harvest-plugin --all-targets -- -D warnings` are both clean.

  **Production confirmation.** This diagnosis and fix were independently corroborated by a live crash report from a deployment on a TLS-enabled Postgres URL: the reported panic location (`establish_migration_connection`'s `handle.block_on(tls::establish(..))` call) and message (`"Cannot start a runtime from within a runtime"`) match exactly, immediately following an `on_startup hook: executing start_harvest_runtime` log line — the precise call site this fix wraps.
- **Phase 4** (next): production hardening -- sharding, observability, metrics, dashboard (Vantage UI — Workers tab shipped in issue #142; DLQ, schedules, and DAG visualization pages remain); Step 5 of issue #256 (remove classic DAG executor, drop `harvest_dag_runs`). Note: the cancellation primitive and `Saga` both ship; their interaction semantics, idempotency contract, and replay-determinism contract are documented in `docs/saga.md` and locked in by three integration tests in `tests/saga_tests.rs` (issue #238).
